Salutation to the Great Elephant-faced One, who dispels the darkness of obstacles, and whose eyes are rippled by a boundless flood of compassion. 1

By me [was praised] the illustrious Ancient Primeval Person,

Strophe 3a:
For the wise, time passes in the diversion of the Vedas and the Shastras.
But for other fools, [death comes] either through sleep or through strife.
Since it has been stated thus, some story that causes wonder in the minds of all people must be told for the purpose of passing the time. Thereupon, the Supreme Lord said to Pārvatī: "O..."
3: "O Mistress of my life, listen; I shall tell you a story that captivates the hearts of all people."

MR Paragraph: 1 The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.”

1. Formerly, on a mountain that served as a touchstone for the armlets upon the arms of the Lord of Laṅkā, 2. the Daughter of the Mountain King addressed the Lord of the World: 3. "O God, there are certain wonderful stories that release one from obstacles."
"Speak to me, who am desirous of hearing, these auspicious words that gladden the mind. Then Mahādeva, with a delighted heart,
spoke to Bhavānī with a voice as sweet as the nectar flowing from the moonbeams upon his head:
7: There is a certain throne, most highly secret;
8: around it are found thirty-two statues of women.
9: Once, at a fitting time, amidst a gathering of those skilled in the arts...
In the midst of King Bhoja’s assembly, they were telling these stories. The Queen said: "O Lord, to whom does this divine seat belong, and what are its characteristics?
Where was it located previously, and under which king's lineage did it belong?"
13: "How did King Bhoja obtain this excellent throne?
This appears like a marvel to me; tell me from the beginning!
14–15: Thus addressed, Mahādeva spoke with the luster of his teeth:
16: Making the moon upon his crown suddenly rise in great splendor.
17: Thus ends the first discourse in the *Siṃhāsanadvātriṃśatikā*.

That which those who know the Vedānta call Brahman, which others call the Pradhāna or the Puruṣa,
or the Lord (Īśvara) as the cause of the universe's emergence—
d: Homage to him, the destroyer of obstacles. 1. Verse 2a:
To the one who brings across people sinking in the ocean of dullness...

Verse 3a:
His own nature consists of bliss, utterly beyond the range of the eyes of even the sages.
We revere the name of Rāma in our hearts, which is the light that illuminates the house of the minds of the wise.
That which shines within the hearts of the virtuous, like the reflection of the moon in water,
is always of the nature of bliss and discernment.
Let us worship the supreme, supreme abode, Śiva. 4.
Stanza: Verse.

Now, for the delight of the wise, a literary composition consisting of both prose and verse is told— a work captivating with the curiosity of the wondrous dialogues of the figures on the thirty-two thrones. And it has been said:

Verse 7.
Once, Gaurī questioned her beloved, who was as white as the moon, as he joyfully wandered while presiding over Kailāsa, which brings delight to the gods.
Having attained yoga through ascetic practices that were difficult to endure, he made all people white with his glories.

O Lord, that some inexplicable power born of my merit awakens within me— something which even ascetics surely cannot attain with their minds— is because I have come into your embrace and am dwelling in happiness. 8

Vikrama-carita: Part No. 2, Chapter: F2 II. Frame-Story: Second Section
King Bhartṛhari and the Fruit that Grants Immortality:
Southern Recension ii (SR)
There is the city of Ujjayinī, vast with all manner of things, its inhabitants surpassing even Indra in their virtues.

There was a city named [Ujjayinī]. Therein lived a king named Bhartṛhari, whose pair of lotus-feet were reddened by the vermilion from the foreheads of all the wives of his vassals; he was proficient in all the arts and learned in all the sciences. His younger brother was named Vikrama, who had seized the prowess of his enemies through his own valor.
There was a man named Bhartṛhari. His wife was named Anaṅgasenā, who surpassed even the celestial nymphs with her virtues such as beauty and grace.
Page: 6 II. Frame-Story: Second Section - sr SR:

In that city, there was a certain Brāhmaṇa who was learned in all the scriptures and especially conversant with the science of mantras; yet he was extremely poor. Through the performance of mantras, he propitiated Bhuvaneśvarī. Satisfied, she said to the Brāhmaṇa: "O Brāhmaṇa, choose a boon."

"Choose a boon. The Brahmin said: "O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, then make me free from old age and death. Thereupon, the Goddess gave him a single divine fruit and said: "O son, eat this fruit; you shall be free from old age and death."

"You shall become [so]. Then the brahmin, having taken that fruit and returned to his own home, bathed, performed the worship of the deities, and just as he was about to eat the fruit, this thought arose in his mind: "Why is it that I am so poor?"
16: "Having become immortal, for whom shall I perform a service? Even for one who lives for a very long time, 17:

the wandering for alms must indeed be performed. Therefore, even a short life is conducive to the welfare of a man who benefits others. Moreover: he who, by means of qualities such as wisdom, power, and so forth..."
19: One who is disciplined lives even for a single moment; his life alone becomes fruitful.
20: And so it has been said:
[Verse 1]
The virtuous declare that the fruit of a man's life is that he lives even for a moment endowed with renowned qualities such as wisdom, heroism, and prosperity.
Even a crow lives for a long time and eats the sacrificial offering. 1.
Stanza: Verse.
And so it is said:
Verse 2:
That life which is lived accompanied by fame and righteousness is a true life; a crow lives long, swallowing putrid scraps of food. 2.
Verse:
Furthermore: Verse: Section 3.1:
Also:
Verse 3:
He alone truly lives, in whose life many others live;
does not even a heron fill its own belly with its beak? 3
Strophe: Verse: Paragraph: 4

There are thousands of base men whose bellies are filled solely by the labor of supporting themselves; but those who, having first satisfied their own needs, strive for the welfare of others, are rare indeed.
He whose own interest is solely the interest of others—that man alone is the leader of the virtuous.
The submarine fire drinks the lord of rivers (the ocean) merely to fill its own insatiable belly, whereas the cloud drinks it to dispel the world's heat accumulated during the summer. 4.
For one who accomplishes no purpose through their birth, actions, or qualities,
there is merely a birth for the sake of designation, like a word used by chance. (5)

Having reflected thus, if that fruit is given to the king, he will become free from old age and death and will righteously protect the fourfold order of society; having taken that fruit,
[the sage] approached the presence of the king.
Wearing a garland of snakes and likewise a body clad in yellow garments—
may Hara and Hari, O protector of the earth, bestow auspiciousness upon you! (6)
Stanza: Verse: Paragraph: 6
Having spoken thus with words of blessing and placed the fruit into the king's hand, he said:
"O King, eat this unprecedented fruit obtained through the grace of a divine boon;
you shall become free from old age and death. Then the king, having taken that fruit, [gave it] to him.

Having granted many agrahāras, he dismissed them and reflected: "Aha! By consuming the fruit of this [act], immortality shall be mine. Yet, I have such great affection for Anaṅgasenā that she will surely die while I am still alive. What agony will that separation cause!"
I am unable to endure it; therefore, this fruit belongs to my beloved granddaughter. (SR Page:
Saying, "I shall give it to Anaṅgasenā," King Bhartṛhari summoned Anaṅgasenā and gave it to her. To her—

Anaṅgasenā had a certain groom as her most beloved; she, having deliberated, gave that fruit to him. That groom had a certain maidservant as his most beloved; he gave it to her. The maidservant, too, felt affection for a certain cowherd; she gave it to him.

He, too, had great affection for a certain cow-dung carrier woman, and he gave it to her. Then that cow-dung carrier woman, having taken the cow dung outside the village and placed the vessel of cow dung upon her head, set that fruit on top of it.

15. Having set it down, while she was coming along the royal road, King Bhartṛhari, together with the princes, was going to the Vaihalī festival; seeing that fruit placed upon a ball of cow dung which had been positioned on her head, he took it and returned home.
Then, having summoned that brahmin, he said: "O brahmin, is there any other fruit such as the one you have given? The brahmin replied:
"O King, that fruit is divine, obtained through the grace of a boon from the deity."
21. No such fruit exists in the world of mortals. Furthermore: Rāma is the Lord himself;
22. falsehood must not be spoken in his presence. He is to be regarded like a god. And so it has been said: 23. [As follows:]

therefore, a wise man should look upon him as a god and should not speak untruthfully to him.

"Was that fruit eaten or not? The king said:
"That fruit was not eaten by me; it was for Anaṅgasenā, who is as dear to me as my own life."

"It was given. The Brahmin said: "In that case, ask her; has that fruit been eaten? Then the king summoned Anaṅgasenā, made her take an oath, and questioned her. She replied: "That fruit was given to the groom. Thereupon—

There is no fortune greater than dispassion, no happiness greater than awakening, no protector other than Hari, and no enemy more formidable than cyclic existence. 18

Having recited this verse, Bhartṛhari attained supreme detachment;
having consecrated Vikramārka upon the throne, he himself departed for the forest.
Thus ends the story of Bhartṛhari’s renunciation.

There is a land of vast prosperity, an ornament of the circle of the earth.
In the victorious city of Ujjayinī, which possesses the auspiciousness of a girdle of excellent mountains,
there was a king named Bhartṛhari, who captivated the hearts of beautiful women; he reigned while his younger brother Vikramāditya served as the obedient crown prince.
5. Anaṅgasenā was the chief queen, the honored and beloved wife of Bhartṛhari;
6. With his heart attached to her, that king knew nothing else. 7. In that very city, there was a certain Brahmin oppressed by misfortune.
Having performed austerities for a long time, he gratified Bhadrakālī.
Urged by the goddess to request a boon for some other purpose,
he forgot his own desire and instead asked for immortality.
11. Then, having given him a divine fruit, the goddess spoke with a smile:
12. "O Brahmin, if you were to eat it, you would become like an immortal.
13. But for two or even for many, this fruit would not yield its fruit."
"This is to be used by one person alone," he said, and immediately vanished.
Then, having reached his own home, his wife came out to meet him with joy.
Page: 9 King Bhartṛhari and the Fruit that Gave Immortality MR:
"What have you obtained, O woman of great wisdom? he asked, inquiring after the fruit of her asceticism.
She, having been made aware of the matter by him with the fruit in his hand, said to him:
"By this very act, you have immediately proven that there is no one who is both learned in the Vedas and wise!"
"19. By you, who possess nothing, who are destined to live long, and who beg everywhere as if you were nearly dead, 20. You exist as one who is practically a corpse.
21. Having heard these words of his wife, he became lost in thought for a long time.
22: Where are the intellect and where are the pleasures for a person devoid of merit (*adṛṣṭa*)?
23: How can one who is destitute and bereft of kin even venture to live?
24: Therefore, I shall give this fruit to the king; let him live.
25. Having thus resolved, the witless man did exactly that;
26. Having received the worship appropriate for him, the brahmin departed from Bhartṛhari. 27. Then, having obtained the reward, the king reflected:
28: "The fruit is for the sole enjoyment of one person," said that best of Brahmins;
29: "Anaṅgasenā has always been my beloved, the giver of my happiness.
30: If she goes to heaven, alas! How shall I endure separation from her?"
31. Thus that lord of the earth gave the divine fruit to his beloved;
32. and she, in turn, presented it to her groom, her most cherished friend.
33. And he, with that very fruit, [rewarded] the sweeper of the stables.
She pleased him, and he in turn pleased his beloved cowherd. Then, at the time of dawn, intending to drive out the herd of cows,
he gave that fruit to his dear wife as she was carrying away cow dung from the pen.
37–38: Carrying a bamboo vessel filled with cow dung and fruit, she began to slowly return to her own dwelling. 39:
At that very moment, King Bhartṛhari then—
40. Coming from the outer garden toward the city, he saw a woman with fruit in her hand.
41. Then, overcome with wonder and still remembering that fruit, 42. he summoned that excellent brahmin, the giver of the fruit, and questioned him.
43–45: "O Brahmin," he said, "the Goddess gave me one fruit. He handed it over and added, "And here is another! Having spoken thus, he showed him the fruit.
Upon examining it and realizing it was indeed so, the wise man spoke to the king:
46: "Surely you have not eaten it; you must have given the fruit to someone. 47: O Lord, ask the Śūdrā specifically why this is so; 48: she will tell you everything, and you will understand."
49. "But you, O Lord of the Earth, are the ruler of the entire world; 50. how could it be possible for anyone to speak falsely in your presence?
51. Thus addressed, the protector of the earth [spoke] to that woman who was carrying cow-dung.
Having summoned her and taken the fruit, he examined it in that very same manner.
Having learned the queen's situation, he spoke these words out of world-weariness:
"By this wicked and exceedingly audacious woman, through the impetuosity of false passion..."
"Alas, I have been deceived by delusion! Fie on this wretched conduct of women!
Having reflected thus for a long time, he attained supreme detachment, consecrated Vikramāditya in his own kingdom, and departed for the forest.
Thus ends the second discourse, titled "The Arising of Dispassion," from the *Vikramādityasiṃhāsanadvātriṃśatikā* by Bhartṛhari.

BR Paragraph: 1 The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.”
1. Īśvara said: In the southern region there is a city named Ujjayinī. There, a king named Bhartṛhari reigned.
Verse 1a:
Like a flower by its fragrance, like the sky by the sun...
By him, O Queen, the city shines like a forest in the springtime.
(Verse 2a:
Endowed with unassuming virtues, he is expert in all branches of political science.
That high-minded one ruled the kingdom, his eyes like those of the *cakora* bird. 2.
Stanza: Verse:
That King Bhartṛhari had a wife named Anaṅgasenā, who was exceedingly beautiful and endowed with great fortune.
Verse 3:
She was a small well of the nectar-essence of the beauty that intoxicates the bodiless god of love;
that fawn-eyed woman was the sole essence of his life. 3
Stanza 4:
Intoxicated by her youth, that young bride shines with her fresh limbs,
like a creeper at the arrival of spring, radiant with its new sprouts.
Verse 5:
Like the moonlight to the moon, or like Sarasvatī to a poet, she became his mistress of life, dearer even than his own life. 5
Stanza: Verse: Paragraph: 3
At that time, in that city, there was a certain Brahmin who, though accomplished in mantras, had by the power of fate become destitute and utterly weak.
(Stanza 6)
O Queen, having attained supreme world-weariness through his state of possessing nothing, that twice-born man propitiated the Goddess, the Sovereign of the World. 6.
Verse 7.
Then, pleased by his state of devotion, the Mother of the World spoke these words: "O wise one, choose a boon.
7 Strophe: 8
Then the twice-born one said to the goddess: "Grant me immortality.
Having replied "Om" to him, Caṇḍī gave him a single divine fruit. (Stanza 9)
a: "As soon as that fruit has been swallowed, immortality shall come to pass";
b: Having heard these words of the goddess, that twice-born man reflected:
(9) Verse:

King Bhartṛhari and the Fruit that Bestowed Immortality Once, while wandering through the forest, King Bhartṛhari came upon a certain tree. Upon seeing it, he thought: "I have heard that there is a fruit here which grants immortality; I must obtain it. He climbed the tree and gathered as many fruits as he could carry. As he descended, he noticed another man approaching from the opposite direction. Seeing him, the king thought: "If I give this fruit to this man, I shall lose my own immortality. With this thought, he threw the fruit down from the tree and continued on his way. Later, as the king was traveling along the road, he encountered a sage who had been practicing austerities for many years. The sage asked him, "O King, why do you appear so dejected? The king replied, "I am weary of worldly existence and desire liberation. The sage said, "If you truly wish for liberation, go to the hermitage of Sage Śukra. There he saw a single fruit hanging from a branch. He thought, "This is surely the fruit that bestows immortality," and he ate it. Immediately, he attained eternal life. Having achieved his purpose, the king returned to his kingdom and ruled with great prosperity. Thus ends the story of King Bhartṛhari and the fruit that bestowed immortality.

IIIb. Frame Story: Third Section, Part 2 – Brief Recension (BR) of iiib: The king said: "O Brahmin, tell me how this came about. The Brahmin replied: "O King, listen. There was once a certain merchant who, having accumulated great wealth through his trade, lived in a city. He had a son named Dhanapāla, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. As he grew up, the youth became skilled in all branches of knowledge and was especially proficient in the science of commerce. One day, while the merchant was away on business, the young man went out to wander the city. There he saw a beautiful woman, the daughter of a wealthy householder, who was adorned with exquisite ornaments and possessed of peerless beauty. Struck by her splendor, he fell deeply in love with her. He sent a messenger to her father, requesting that she be given to him in marriage. The householder agreed, saying, 'I shall give her to you, provided you can bring me a certain rare gem from a distant land. Determined to fulfill his promise, the youth set out on a long journey across the sea. After many hardships, he reached a magnificent island where he found a great temple dedicated to the goddess Lakṣmī. There, he met a wise sage who told him of a hidden treasure beneath the temple, guarded by a fierce serpent. The sage instructed him to offer a sacrifice of flowers and incense to appease the serpent and thus gain access to the jewel. Following these instructions, Dhanapāla performed the rites. The serpent, pleased by his devotion, revealed the jewel to him. Taking it, the youth returned home safely and presented it to the merchant’s householder. The householder was delighted and gave his daughter in marriage to Dhanapāla. They lived together in great happiness for some time. However, one day, as they were walking in the garden, the young wife noticed a mark on her husband's forehead—a sign of his travels—that reminded her of her own past life. She asked him about it, and he told her the entire story of his quest for the jewel. Filled with wonder, she recalled her previous birth as a celestial nymph who had been cursed to become human. Through their conversation, they realized they were karmic siblings from a former life. Their reunion brought them even greater joy, and they lived out their lives in harmony, supported by the wealth they had acquired through righteous means. The king said: "It is wonderful how even those who have fallen into the cycle of rebirth can find such fortune through merit. Tell me, O Brahmin, what further lesson does this story convey? The Brahmin replied: "O King, this story teaches that through perseverance, wisdom, and devotion, one may overcome obstacles and attain the fruits of one's desires. Furthermore, it shows that the bonds of affection formed in previous lives can manifest again in this world, leading to lasting happiness.
Thus ends the third section, part two, of the frame story in the Brief Recension.

Frame-Story: Fourth Section [The King] said: "O wise one, tell me how this matter was resolved. The minister replied: "O Great King, listen. In this world, there is a city named Vārāṇasī. There dwelt a king named Mahendrasena, who was a devotee of Śiva. He had a son named Indrasena, who was handsome and beloved by the people. Once, while wandering about, the prince saw a certain woman of exquisite beauty. Struck by her loveliness, he was overcome by passion and, having no other recourse, took her by force. When she cried out for help, her kinsmen gathered and seized the prince. They brought him before the king and said: 'O King, this son of yours has committed a great crime; he has violated a woman of our family. Therefore, let him be punished according to the law. The king, being devoted to righteousness, reflected: 'If I do not punish my own son, the people will lose faith in me and say that I am partial. Yet, if I kill my son, I shall incur the sin of matricide and be reborn in hell. What should I do? While the king was thus deliberating, a voice from the sky spoke: 'O King, do not act rashly. This is a test of your wisdom. If you spare your son, you shall attain supreme sovereignty; if you execute him, you shall fall into hell. Hearing this divine voice, the king, with a heart full of compassion, released his son. Because of that act of mercy, the king attained the highest state. Thus, O King, one should always practice compassion toward all living beings. The King said: "This is indeed wonderful. But tell me, what did the other two ministers do? The minister replied: "O King, they both acted with malice. One of them, seeing a man who had stolen a cow, killed him immediately. The other, seeing a man who had stolen gold, executed him after a long period of investigation. Both of them, due to their violent deeds, fell into hell. Therefore, O King, one should never act with haste or cruelty, but should always govern with wisdom and compassion. The King, having heard this, was greatly pleased and honored the minister. Thus ends the fourth section of the frame-story.

1 The first section of the *Jñānasiddhi* (JR) begins with an homage to the primordial wisdom of the Buddhas, which is free from conceptual elaborations and is the source of all enlightened qualities. It then proceeds to explain that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is beyond the reach of dualistic thought and linguistic expression, being characterized by the non-duality of subject and object. This state is described as the natural luminosity of the mind, which, when realized, liberates one from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). The text emphasizes that this realization is not attained through external rituals or intellectual analysis alone, but through the internal cultivation of the path of skillful means and wisdom. Thus, the practitioner is instructed to integrate the view of emptiness with the compassionate activity of benefiting others, thereby attaining the state of a Vajradhara.

V. Frame Story: Fifth Section—The Finding of the Throne by Bhoja (Southern Recension) Once upon a time, King Bhoja, having heard of the miraculous throne, set out from his capital with a vast army to seek it. After traveling for many days, he reached a dense forest where he encountered a great sage. Bowing low, the king asked him for guidance as to how he might find the throne. The sage replied, "O King, you shall find the throne at the foot of a banyan tree in a secluded grove. However, it is guarded by a fierce Yakṣa named Mahābala. You must first subdue him through your prowess before you may take possession of the throne. Following the sage’s instructions, Bhoja proceeded to the designated spot. There, he beheld the magnificent throne, radiant and adorned with jewels, standing beneath the banyan tree. As he approached, the Yakṣa emerged from the shadows, roaring with a terrifying voice and brandishing a mace. A fierce battle ensued between the king and the Yakṣa. Through his skill in weaponry and divine grace, Bhoja overcame the demon and brought him under his control. Having subdued the guardian, the king ascended the throne. At that very moment, the entire assembly of gods descended from the heavens and showered flowers upon him. The celestial chariot appeared, and the gods proclaimed: "O King, this is the Throne of Glory; whoever sits upon it shall become a universal sovereign. Bhoja, having obtained the throne, returned to his kingdom in triumph. There, he ruled with justice and prosperity, his reign marked by peace and abundance. Thus ends the fifth section of the Frame Story, concerning the finding of the throne by Bhoja.

In the city of Vidarbha, there was a king named Bhoja, who was a sovereign of the whole earth, possessed of great power and virtue. He was devoted to the service of his father and mother, ever intent on the welfare of his subjects, and a protector of the four castes and stages of life. Once, while wandering through the forest for the sake of hunting, he reached a secluded grove filled with various trees and creepers. There, in the midst of a dense thicket, he beheld a magnificent throne, radiant with jewels and fashioned from celestial gold. Seeing that wonderful seat, the king, filled with curiosity, approached it and sat upon it; yet, as soon as he sat, he fell down unconscious. Regaining his senses after a moment, the king rose up and, seeing the throne empty, reflected within himself: 'This throne is surely not of human origin; it must belong to some god or to a great sage. I shall not depart from this place until I have discovered its secret and the one who is worthy to sit upon it. The ascetic, wearing matted hair and bark garments, carrying a staff and a water-pot, arrived at that spot where the king stood. Frame Story: Seventh Section Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Pāṭaliputra. He was a man of great power and majesty, possessing a vast army and many elephants, horses, and chariots. His kingdom was prosperous and free from all disturbances, and he governed it with righteousness. Now, that king had a son named Candraprabha, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by the people. The prince was well-versed in the sciences and skilled in the arts. One day, while wandering about the city for recreation, he saw a merchant’s daughter named Śrīmatī. She was exceedingly beautiful, like a goddess descended to earth, and her grace captivated the hearts of all who beheld her. Candraprabha, struck by her beauty, became deeply enamored of her. He sent messengers to inquire after her, and eventually, through the mediation of a trusted friend, he was granted permission to marry her. The wedding was celebrated with great splendor, and the two lived together in happiness. However, as time passed, the king Mahāsena grew old and infirm, and he realized that his end was near. Knowing that his son Candraprabha was capable of ruling, he summoned him and said, "My son, I have grown weak and my life is drawing to a close. I wish to retire from the affairs of state and devote myself to spiritual practices. Therefore, I entrust this kingdom to you; rule it with justice and protect your subjects. Candraprabha bowed before his father and accepted the burden of sovereignty. Having installed his son on the throne, King Mahāsena retired to the forest to live as an ascetic. Meanwhile, Prince Candraprabha, though established in power, remained devoted to virtue. He governed the kingdom righteously, and his subjects prospered under his rule. Yet, despite his efforts, he found no peace of mind, for he was constantly troubled by the thought of his wife Śrīmatī. He wondered whether she was truly faithful or if her heart might be turned elsewhere. One day, while seated in his palace, he heard a voice from the sky speaking these verses: "O King, do not let your mind be troubled by doubt regarding your wife. She is chaste and pure, devoted solely to you, like a lotus in the water. Her heart is fixed on you alone, and she remains steadfast in her vows. Cast away this anxiety, O Lord of Men, and enjoy your life in peace. Upon hearing these words, Candraprabha was filled with joy. He understood that his wife was indeed virtuous and free from any blemish. From that time forth, he ruled his kingdom with even greater diligence, honoring his father's legacy and ensuring the welfare of all his subjects. Thus ends the seventh section of the frame story.

JR Paragraph: 1 The first section of the *Jñānasiddhi* (The Accomplishment of Gnosis). Homage to the Venerable Vajrayoginī! In this world, there are many who desire liberation; yet, among those who seek it, few truly attain it. Why is this? Because they do not know the essential point of the path. Therefore, I shall explain the method for accomplishing the supreme siddhi, which is the essence of all tantras and the heart-essence of all yogas. Listen with one-pointed attention! First, the practitioner should select a secluded place that is free from disturbances and conducive to meditation. There, having prepared a comfortable seat, he should assume the vajra posture (*vajrāsana*) or the lotus posture (*padmāsana*). Then, generating the altruistic intention (*bodhicitta*) to liberate all sentient beings, he should visualize the mandala of his chosen deity. Within the center of a pure and radiant palace, he should meditate upon the seed-syllable of the deity. From that syllable, light rays radiate forth, inviting the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) from the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*). He should then cause the wisdom-being to enter into union with the visualized commitment-being (*samayasattva*), and through the offering of the five nectars and the four mudrās, he should worship the deity with intense devotion. Next, reciting the mantra of the deity with unwavering concentration, he should perform the practice of the "inner fire" (*caṇḍālī*) to melt the essence-drops (*bindu*). As these drops descend through the central channel, he should experience the four joys (*caturānanda*). By means of this, he will gradually realize the stages of the path, culminating in the attainment of the state of a Vidyādhara. Thus, by following this method, even one who is dull-witted may swiftly achieve the supreme accomplishment. This is the secret instruction of the masters, the very life-force of the Vajrayāna. The Story of the First Statuette: Vikrama’s Rule for Giving Alms Southern Recension of 1 Once, when King Vikramāditya was ruling the earth, he issued a royal decree that no one should give alms to mendicants except at his own door. One day, a certain mendicant, having heard of this proclamation, went to the king’s palace gate. Seeing the king seated upon his throne, he recited a verse: “O King, you who are the refuge of the world, The giver of wealth and the protector of the earth, If you do not grant me alms today, Then where else shall I go for sustenance? Hearing these words, the king, moved by compassion, gave him a handful of gold coins. The mendicant, delighted, departed. However, another mendicant, hearing of this, approached the king with a similar request. The king, wishing to maintain consistency, gave him the same amount. This continued until many mendicants had come and received gifts. Then a certain wise man, observing the king’s conduct, spoke to him: “Your Majesty, it is said that a gift given without discrimination is like water poured into the ocean—it benefits neither the giver nor the recipient. Therefore, you should establish a system of distribution. The king agreed and ordered that from that day forward, all mendicants should assemble at the palace gate at a fixed time, and the king would distribute alms according to their needs and merit. Thus, the king’s reputation for generosity spread throughout the land, and his rule became even more illustrious. Thus ends the first story of the Vikrama-carita.

The Story of the Second Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāśakti who ruled over the city of Śrāvastī. He was a righteous ruler who governed his kingdom with justice and compassion. His queen was named Śrīmatī, and they had a son named Candraprabha, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, as the prince was wandering through the royal gardens, he encountered a group of wandering mendicants. They were emaciated from hunger and thirst, their robes tattered and their bodies covered in dust. Seeing them, the prince’s heart was filled with compassion. He approached them and asked, "O holy ones, why do you wander thus, suffering such hardship? The mendicants replied, "Prince, we are seekers of the Dharma. We wander from place to place to hear the teachings of the Buddhas and to practice the path of virtue. The prince said, "If that is so, then may I serve you? Please accept my offerings of food and drink, for I wish to gain merit. The mendicants accepted his invitation, and the prince provided them with excellent food and water. As they ate, the prince sat before them and listened intently to their discourse on the Dharma. After they had finished eating, the prince requested, "Venerable sirs, please grant me a teaching that will lead to liberation. One of the elders replied, "Prince, the root of all suffering is attachment to worldly pleasures. To overcome this, one must cultivate mindfulness and renounce all desire for sensory gratification. The prince was deeply moved by these words. He returned to the palace and informed his father of his desire to renounce the world and seek the path of enlightenment. However, King Mahāśakti, out of love for his son, refused to grant him permission. Undeterred, the prince continued to practice virtue in secret. He gave away his wealth to the poor, honored the monks, and lived a life of restraint. One day, while walking through the city, he saw a beggar who was emaciated and covered in sores. Feeling great pity, the prince offered him gold coins and garments. As the prince was returning home, he heard the sound of a woman’s lamentation. He went to investigate and found her weeping beside a well. She told him that she was the wife of a merchant who had recently died, leaving her destitute and alone. The prince took her to his palace and provided her with all the necessities of life. He treated her with kindness and respect, and she became a devoted follower of the Dharma. Years passed, and the prince remained steadfast in his commitment to virtue. One night, as he lay awake, he heard a voice in the sky saying, "Candraprabha, your merit is vast. In time, you shall attain Buddhahood. Filled with joy, the prince resolved to leave the household life. With the blessing of the gods, he was able to persuade his father to allow him to become a monk. He shaved his head, donned the saffron robes, and set out on his journey to find a spiritual teacher. Along the way, he encountered many obstacles, but through his unwavering resolve and the power of his past merits, he overcame them all. Finally, he arrived at a forest hermitage where he met the venerable Ācārya Śāntideva. Under his guidance, the prince practiced meditation and perfected the six perfections. After many years of diligent practice, he attained the realization of emptiness and became a fully enlightened Buddha. His name was Candraprabha-jina, and he taught the Dharma to countless beings, leading them across the ocean of suffering to the shore of liberation. Thus ends the story of the second statuette. It teaches that even those in the midst of worldly pleasures can achieve enlightenment through compassion, virtue, and the cultivation of wisdom. Those who follow the example of Prince Candraprabha will surely find the path to true happiness.

The Story of the Second Statuette – br, jr Brief Recension of 2 The second statuette said: "O King, listen to this ancient tale. There was once a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Pāṭaliputra. He had a son named Candraprabha, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by the people. The sage, seeing the prince, spoke to him with affection: 'O Prince, you are endowed with beauty, youth, and noble lineage; why do you not enjoy the pleasures of the world? For the wise say that youth is like a flash of lightning, and life is as transient as a drop of dew on a blade of grass. The prince replied: 'O Holy One, I am not ignorant of these things; however, my mind is set upon the attainment of liberation. Worldly pleasures are as fleeting as bubbles on water and lead only to suffering. Hearing this, the sage was filled with wonder and said: 'It is rare indeed to find one so resolute in the midst of worldly distractions. I shall grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire. The prince requested: 'May I possess such wisdom and discernment that I may never fall under the sway of passion or delusion. The sage granted his wish. Later, the prince returned to his capital. There, he heard of a courtesan named Manoharā, renowned for her beauty and charm. Driven by curiosity, he went to her abode. Upon seeing her, he was immediately struck by her allure, and his resolve wavered. Remembering the sage’s boon, he reflected: 'How can I remain firm when faced with such temptation? At that moment, a voice from the sky proclaimed: 'O Prince, remember your vow! This woman is but a phantom created by Māra to test your resolve. Realizing this, the prince summoned his courage and departed. Meanwhile, the courtesan, unable to contain her passion, disguised herself as a young Brahmin girl and followed him. When the prince saw her, he thought: 'This must be a trick of Māra. He then recited a verse: "Like a dream at dawn, like a painted city in the sky, Like a mirage in the desert, so are these sensual delights. Having spoken thus, he turned away. The disguised girl then revealed her true form and begged for mercy. Moved by compassion, the prince granted her freedom from her former life of vice. She took refuge in the Dharma and became a devoted follower. Thus, O King, even those of great merit can be led astray by the power of passion; therefore, one must always guard the mind with vigilance. The second statuette concluded its story. The king, hearing this, was deeply moved and praised the prince’s steadfastness. He then commanded his ministers to search for the sage who had bestowed the boon, so that he might honor him and seek further instruction. The ministers departed to fulfill his command.

The Sea God’s Gift of the Four Magic Jewels (Cintāmaṇi) [The Buddha said: "In the past, there was a king named Śubhavyūha. He ruled over Jambudvīpa, which was filled with the seven precious jewels. His kingdom was vast and his wealth was immeasurable. He possessed a great army and many attendants; he governed according to the Dharma and protected his subjects with righteousness. At that time, the king had a son named Candraprabha. From the moment he was born, he was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. He was wise, intelligent, and possessed of great compassion. He took pleasure in giving charity and sought to hear the sublime Dharma. One day, the prince went out for a stroll and saw a poor man who was emaciated, suffering, and covered in sores. Seeing him, the prince felt deep pity and asked, ‘Why are you so miserable? The man replied, ‘I am poor and have no means of livelihood. I have no food or clothing, and I suffer from hunger and cold. The prince said, ‘I shall give you whatever you need. He then gave the man gold, silver, pearls, and various treasures, as well as garments and food. Having satisfied the man, the prince continued on his way. As he traveled, he encountered a great ocean. On the shore stood a deity, the Lord of the Ocean, who held four precious wish-fulfilling jewels (cintāmaṇi). The deity said to the prince, ‘O Prince, these four jewels possess inconceivable power. The first fulfills all desires; the second brings rain at will; the third provides all medicinal herbs; and the fourth grants long life and health. If you take them, you shall rule over the entire world and bring peace to all beings. The prince thought to himself, ‘If I were to accept these jewels, I would surely gain great power and wealth. However, I have heard the teachings of the Buddhas of the three times: they renounce worldly pleasures and seek only the path of liberation. If I remain attached to these jewels, I will never be able to attain enlightenment. With this thought, the prince refused the jewels. The deity of the ocean was amazed and said, ‘O Prince, you are truly rare! You possess a mind of supreme purity and are not moved by worldly gain. Because of your merit, you shall soon attain the state of a Buddha. Having spoken thus, the deity offered the four jewels to the prince and vanished. The prince took the jewels and returned to his father, the King Śubhavyūha. He presented the jewels to the king and explained what had happened. The king was filled with joy and said, ‘My son has performed a most difficult deed. By rejecting these jewels, he has shown that his heart is set on the supreme Dharma. The prince then used the power of the jewels to provide for the needs of all living beings, yet he remained detached from their influence. Eventually, he renounced the throne, left the household life, and practiced the path under the guidance of the Buddhas. After countless eons of cultivation, he attained perfect enlightenment and became a Buddha known as Candrasūryapradīpa. The Buddha said to the assembly: “That Prince Candraprabha was none other than myself in a former life. Because I rejected those four jewels and did not cling to worldly power, I have now attained the wisdom of a Buddha. Therefore, you should know that one who seeks the Dharma must always practice detachment and generosity, even toward the most precious things.”

**Jainistic Recension of 3 JR:** In this world, there are four types of living beings (*jīva*): those who possess bodies, those who do not possess bodies, those who are both, and those who are neither. Among these, those who possess bodies are further divided into two categories: those with form (*mūrta*) and those without form (*amūrta*). Those without form are of two kinds: those that are conscious (*cetana*) and those that are unconscious (*acetana*). Among these, the unconscious ones are of two kinds: eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). The eternal ones are of two kinds: those that are subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and those that are not subject to transformation (*apariṇāmin*). Those that are not subject to transformation are of two kinds: those that are characterized by existence (*astitva*) and those that are characterized by non-existence (*nāstitva*). Those that are characterized by existence are of two kinds: those that are characterized by permanence (*nityatva*) and those that are characterized by impermanence (*anityatva*). Those that are characterized by permanence are of two kinds: those that are characterized by unity (*ekatva*) and those that are characterized by plurality (*anekatva*). Those that are characterized by unity are of two kinds: those that are characterized by simplicity (*asādhāraṇa*) and those that are characterized by commonality (*sādhāraṇa*). Those that are characterized by simplicity are of two kinds: those that are characterized by singularity (*kevala*) and those that are characterized by multiplicity (*saṅkhyeya*). Those that are characterized by singularity are of two kinds: those that are characterized by infinitude (*ananta*) and those that are characterized by finitude (*asaṅkhyeya*). Those that are characterized by infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by spatial infinitude (*deśānanta*) and those that are characterized by temporal infinitude (*kālānanta*). Those that are characterized by temporal infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by absolute infinitude (*sarvathānanta*) and those that are characterized by relative infinitude (*bhāvānanta*). Those that are characterized by relative infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by internal infinitude (*antarānanta*) and those that are characterized by external infinitude (*bahiraṅgānanta*). Those that are characterized by external infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by objective infinitude (*viṣayānanta*) and those that are characterized by subjective infinitude (*svabhāvānanta*). Those that are characterized by subjective infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by pure infinitude (*śuddhānanta*) and those that are characterized by impure infinitude (*aśuddhānanta*). Those that are characterized by impure infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by limited infinitude (*paricchinnānanta*) and those that are characterized by unlimited infinitude (*aparicchinnānanta*). Those that are characterized by unlimited infinitude are of two kinds: those that are characterized by infinite space (*ākāśānanta*) and those that are characterized by infinite time (*kālananta*). Those that are characterized by infinite time are of two kinds: those that are characterized by past time (*atītakāla*) and those that are characterized by future time (*anāgatakāla*). Those that are characterized by future time are of two kinds: those that are characterized by the beginningless (*anādika*) and those that are characterized by the endless (*anantika*). Those that are characterized by the endless are of two kinds: those that are characterized by the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and those that are characterized by the manifest (*vyakta*). Those that are characterized by the manifest are of two kinds: those that are characterized by the gross (*sthūla*) and those that are characterized by the subtle (*sūkṣma*). Those that are characterized by the subtle are of two kinds: those that are characterized by the atomic (*paramāṇu*) and those that are characterized by the composite (*saṃghāta*). Those that are characterized by the composite are of two kinds: those that are characterized by the homogeneous (*samāna*) and those that are characterized by the heterogeneous (*visama*). Those that are characterized by the heterogeneous are of two kinds: those that are characterized by the simple (*kevala*) and those that are characterized by the complex (*miśra*).
Those that are characterized by the complex are of two kinds:

4. The Story of the Fourth Statuette The king asked: "What is this? The statuette replied: "O King, listen. In the city of Kāñcī there was a merchant named Dhanapāla. He had a son named Guṇapāla, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. He was skilled in all branches of learning and possessed great wealth. One day, while wandering about, he saw a beautiful maiden of noble birth. Struck by her beauty, he fell deeply in love with her. He sent a messenger to her father and requested her hand in marriage. The father agreed, saying, 'She shall be given to him, provided that he can bring a golden lotus from Lake Manasa. Guṇapāla set out for the north. After traveling for many days, he reached a forest where he encountered a group of merchants. They traveled together until they arrived at the shore of a vast ocean. There, they found a ship ready to depart. As they were about to set sail, a voice from the sky proclaimed: 'O merchants, do not enter this sea! For within it dwells a great serpent-king named Śaṅkhacūḍa, who will surely destroy you all. Despite these warnings, the merchants insisted on sailing. As the ship entered the waters, a fierce storm arose, and the vessel began to sink. Guṇapāla, seeing his companions perishing, prayed to the gods. By the power of his merit, a divine being appeared and rescued the ship, bringing it safely to the shore of a distant island. There, Guṇapāla rested. While wandering about, he came upon a beautiful garden. In its center stood a magnificent palace, and within it, a woman of exquisite beauty was sitting alone, weeping. Approaching her, he asked, 'Who are you, and why do you weep? She replied, 'I am the daughter of the Naga king Śaṅkhacūḍa. My name is Padmāvatī. My father has commanded me to guard this golden lotus, which grows here. However, I have fallen in love with a mortal man and am grieving because I cannot be with him. Guṇapāla revealed his identity and said, 'I am that very man who has come here seeking the golden lotus. I am your husband. She was overjoyed and led him to her father. The Naga king welcomed him and gave him the golden lotus. With the lotus in hand, Guṇapāla returned home. His father-in-law, the merchant, was delighted and gave him a great dowry. Guṇapāla lived happily with his wife, enjoying all the pleasures of the world. The king asked, "Did he succeed in his quest? The statuette replied, "Yes, O King, he did. But listen further: one day, as Guṇapāla was walking in the palace gardens, he saw a beautiful woman coming toward him. She was the daughter of a neighboring king, and she had been sent by her father to choose a husband. Seeing Guṇapāla, she fell in love with him instantly. She sent a messenger to request his hand in marriage. Her father agreed, and the wedding was celebrated with great splendor. After some time, the king of that land died, and his ministers installed Guṇapāla as the new ruler. Thus, through his own merit and wisdom, he attained sovereignty and lived in happiness. The king remarked, "It is wonderful how one who possesses virtue and intelligence overcomes all obstacles. The statuette concluded, "Indeed, O King, those who are endowed with virtue, wisdom, and perseverance never fail to achieve their goals. Thus ends the story of the fourth statuette.

The Story of the Fourth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and possessed of immense wealth, yet he was devoid of all virtue. His subjects were constantly oppressed by his harsh punishments and his greed for wealth. In that same city lived a merchant’s son named Guṇākara, who was upright, virtuous, and compassionate. He was devoted to his parents and always acted with integrity. One day, while wandering through the marketplace, he saw a poor, elderly woman selling her wares. Moved by pity, he gave her a portion of his own food. Later, as Guṇākara was walking along the road, he encountered a man who had lost his way in the forest. Without hesitation, Guṇākara guided him back to the city, providing him with food and shelter until he could find his own path. Meanwhile, the king, having heard of these acts of kindness, summoned Guṇākara to his presence. "I have heard," the king said, "that you have been generous to the poor and helpful to strangers. Tell me, what is it that you desire? I shall grant you whatever you ask. Guṇākara replied, "Your Majesty, I have no desire for wealth or power. I only wish that you might rule with justice and compassion, treating all your subjects with kindness. The king, enraged by this answer, ordered his guards to cast Guṇākara into a dark dungeon, saying, "Let this man remain there until he learns the lesson of obedience. Guṇākara, however, remained undaunted. From within the dungeon, he continued to recite sacred verses and offer prayers for the welfare of the king and his kingdom. His devotion moved the hearts of the gods, and one night, a deity appeared before him. "O noble youth," the deity said, "your virtues are known to me. I shall grant you a boon. Choose whatever you desire. Guṇākara replied, "If you are pleased with me, O Lord, then let the king become a righteous ruler, and let my parents live long and in peace. The deity granted his request, and immediately the king’s heart was softened. He released Guṇākara from prison and restored him to his former status. From that time forward, King Mahāsena ruled with wisdom and mercy, and the land of Vārāṇasī became a place of prosperity and happiness once more. Thus ends the story of the fourth statuette. It teaches that even in the face of adversity, a virtuous person remains steadfast in their goodness, and that true greatness lies not in power, but in compassion for others.

The story of the fourth statuette is as follows: Once upon a time, there lived a certain merchant who was very wealthy. He had a son named Jayasena, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, the merchant fell ill and, knowing his end was near, summoned his son and said: "My dear son, I have accumulated much wealth through honest means. I wish to ensure that it remains within our family and does not pass to strangers. Jayasena replied with humility: "Father, I shall do as you command. I will take care of this wealth and ensure it is preserved for our lineage. After some time, the merchant passed away. Jayasena took charge of the estate and managed the household with great diligence. However, he was naturally inclined toward generosity and compassion. He would often give alms to the poor and support those in need, even at the expense of his own resources. As years passed, the family fortune began to dwindle. His relatives and servants, seeing his constant giving, grew resentful. They whispered among themselves: "This Jayasena is a fool. He squanders the wealth his father labored so hard to acquire. Soon, we shall be left destitute. One day, a close relative approached Jayasena and said: "Nephew, you must stop this reckless spending. Your father’s wealth is being exhausted by your charity. You must learn to be more prudent and look after your own interests. Jayasena listened patiently and replied: "Uncle, I understand your concern. However, my father taught me that wealth is meant to be shared, not hoarded. It is better to lose it through virtue than to preserve it through stinginess. Despite his nephew's firm resolve, the family situation continued to decline. Eventually, they were forced to sell their lands and possessions to survive. One evening, as Jayasena sat alone in his chamber, he reflected on his life. He thought: "I have followed the path of righteousness, yet I am now destitute. What is the purpose of virtue if it leads to such hardship? In his distress, he resolved to abandon his charitable ways and focus solely on his own welfare. From that moment, he became miserly and withheld even the small comforts of his household. Meanwhile, a wise old man who had known the merchant’s family for many years visited Jayasena. Seeing his transformation, the elder sighed and said: "Alas, Jayasena! You have forgotten the true meaning of wealth. It is not merely the accumulation of gold and grain, but the joy it brings when shared with others. Your father’s legacy was not just material; it was a testament to his character. By abandoning virtue, you have lost far more than your fortune. Jayasena listened to the elder’s words and felt a deep sense of remorse. He realized that true wealth lies not in possession, but in the purity of one’s intentions. He returned to his former ways, opening his heart once more to generosity and kindness. In time, through his renewed commitment to virtue, his reputation was restored, and his family’s fortunes gradually recovered. Jayasena learned that while external wealth may fluctuate, the inner wealth of integrity and compassion remains steadfast. Thus ends the story of the fourth statuette.
It teaches that true prosperity is rooted in moral conduct and selfless service, for it is through such virtues that one finds lasting fulfillment.

5. The Story of the Fifth Statuette. Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāśakti who ruled over the city of Śrāvastī. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. However, he was not satisfied with his own strength; he desired to conquer all the kings of Jambudvīpa. Having assembled a great host of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers, he set out on a campaign of conquest. As he marched through the land, he subdued many kingdoms one after another until he reached the border of a certain forest. There, he encountered a formidable enemy king who had gathered a vast force. A fierce battle ensued, and for many days the two armies fought without respite. In the midst of the conflict, King Mahāśakti’s army suffered a great defeat. His forces were broken, and he himself was surrounded by the enemy. Seeing his situation dire, the king resolved to fight to the death rather than surrender. He drew his sword and charged into the thick of the fray. As he advanced, he encountered a lone warrior of immense prowess. The two combatants engaged in a duel that lasted for hours. Finally, the enemy king struck a decisive blow, and King Mahāśakti fell to the ground, mortally wounded. Before he passed away, the dying king summoned his remaining loyal ministers and said to them: "I have conquered many lands, yet I have failed in my ultimate goal. My life is at its end, and I am about to depart this world. I leave behind no heir to carry on my lineage. Therefore, I entrust you with this task: take my body and place it upon a high mountain peak so that it may be seen from afar. Furthermore, construct a magnificent statue of me in gold and install it in a temple, so that people may remember my deeds. The ministers wept bitterly at these words, but they honored their lord’s final wish. They carried his remains to the mountain and erected a grand monument. They then commissioned artisans to fashion a golden statue of the king, which was installed in a temple built in his honor. Years passed, and the kingdom eventually fell into decline. The people forgot the deeds of their former ruler, and the temple began to fall into ruin. One day, a wandering ascetic arrived at the site. He saw the crumbling temple and the neglected statue, and he felt a surge of compassion. He resolved to restore the site to its former glory. With the help of a devoted layman, the ascetic repaired the temple and cleaned the statue. He then made offerings of flowers and incense before the image, praying for the king’s welfare. As he performed his devotions, he noticed something extraordinary: whenever he offered a flower, the statue would move its head slightly to receive it. Filled with wonder, the ascetic realized that the king’s merit was still potent. He understood that the king’s spirit remained watchful over his realm. From that day forward, the ascetic and the layman continued their service, and the temple became a place of pilgrimage once more. This is the story of King Mahāśakti, whose memory endured through the power of his own resolve and the devotion of those who came after him. It teaches that even in the face of defeat and death, a noble heart can leave a lasting legacy.
Thus ends the story of the fifth statuette.

5. The Story of the Fifth Statuette: The Dilemma of the Jewel-Bearer Southern Recension of 5 Once upon a time, there lived a merchant who was a great friend of the Bodhisattva. He had a son named Maṇibhadra, who was exceedingly clever and wise. One day, while traveling abroad, the merchant fell ill and died. His wife, overwhelmed by grief, wept bitterly and lamented. Then Maṇibhadra said to her, "Mother, do not grieve so. I shall provide for you. With these words, he took his father’s wealth and set out on a journey to a foreign land. After some time, he arrived at a city where he found a great merchant who was a friend of his father. He stayed with him for a while, and eventually, having gained much wealth through trade, he prepared to return home. As he was about to depart, the merchant friend said to him, "My dear Maṇibhadra, take this casket of jewels; it is filled with priceless gems. Keep it with great care, for it is of immense value. Maṇibhadra accepted the gift and set out on his journey back. On the way, he encountered a band of robbers. They surrounded him and said, "Hand over your wealth, or else you shall die! Maṇibhadra replied, "I have nothing but this body and this casket of jewels. Take whatever you wish, but let me go. The robbers seized his clothes and ornaments, but they would not let him go. Then Maṇibhadra thought to himself, "If I give up this casket, I shall lose my life. But if I keep it, I shall surely be killed. What course of action should I take? He reflected deeply on the dilemma. At that moment, a deity who had been his friend in a previous life appeared before him and said, "Maṇibhadra, do not be distressed. I shall help you. Cast this casket into the river; it will float away safely. You must follow it, keeping your eyes fixed upon it, until you reach the other bank. There, you will find a man carrying a load of firewood. Give him the casket, and he will take you to your home. Maṇibhadra followed the deity’s instructions. He threw the casket into the river and followed it as it floated downstream. When he reached the opposite bank, he saw a woodcutter approaching. He gave the casket to the woodcutter, who took it and carried him to his own village. There, the woodcutter introduced him to his family, saying, "This is a noble youth who has come to us for refuge. The woodcutter’s family treated Maṇibhadra with great hospitality. After some time, the woodcutter went to the market to sell his wood. Maṇibhadra, seeing an opportunity, took the casket and fled. He returned to his own country and presented the casket to his mother. She was overjoyed and said, "My son, you have truly fulfilled your promise. Meanwhile, the merchant friend who had given him the jewels heard what had happened. He sent a messenger to Maṇibhadra, saying, "My dear friend, why did you abandon the casket? It was filled with the most precious gems. Return it to me. Maṇibhadra replied, "Friend, I abandoned the casket because I feared for my life. I could not bear the thought of losing both my life and my virtue. Therefore, I left it behind. The merchant friend was amazed by Maṇibhadra’s wisdom and integrity. He praised him greatly and, having no further need for the casket, allowed Maṇibhadra to keep it. Thus, Maṇibhadra lived happily, having resolved his dilemma through wisdom and virtue. The moral of the story is that one should always act with discernment when faced with a difficult choice, weighing the consequences of each path and choosing that which preserves both life and virtue. Thus ends the story of the fifth statuette.

**The Story of the Fifth Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king named Śūradatta who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and majesty, possessed of a vast army and many elephants, horses, and chariots. His kingdom was prosperous, free from calamity, and filled with abundant grain. He was devoted to the practice of dharma and protected his subjects with righteousness. Now, that king had a queen named Yaśodharā, who was endowed with every virtue and beauty. She was dear to him as his own life. However, she was childless; though she longed for a son, her wish remained unfulfilled. One day, the king, overcome by grief at being without an heir, went to the park outside the city. There he saw a great sage seated beneath a tree, absorbed in meditation. Approaching him with humility, the king paid his respects and sat down before him. The sage, perceiving the king’s distress, spoke to him with words of consolation: “O King, do not grieve. By the power of my asceticism, I shall grant you a son who will be a source of joy to the entire world. Delighted by these words, the king returned to his palace. Soon thereafter, through the grace of the sage, the queen conceived a child. When the pregnancy reached its full term, she gave birth to a son of extraordinary splendor. Because he was born while his mother was in a state of great joy (*yaśa*), they named him Yaśodhara. As the prince grew, he was instructed in all the sciences and arts. He became skilled in horsemanship, archery, and the use of weapons, as well as in statecraft and the duties of a king. He was beloved by the people and held in high esteem by his father. One day, the king summoned his ministers and said, “I have grown old, and I desire to retire from the affairs of state. I wish to install my son Yaśodhara as the crown prince and entrust the burden of the kingdom to him. The ministers, seeing the king’s resolve, agreed to his proposal. On an auspicious day, the prince was invested with the insignia of royalty and installed as the heir apparent. From that time on, the young king governed the realm with wisdom and compassion, delighting both his subjects and his father. Thus ends the story of the fifth statuette.

The Story of the Seventh Statuette. Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahendrasena who ruled over the city of Kāñcanapura. He was a man of great virtue, devoted to righteousness, and possessed of immense wealth and power. His queen, named Śrīmatī, was his equal in beauty and character, and together they lived in perfect harmony. One day, while wandering through the royal gardens, the king beheld a beautiful lotus pond filled with blooming lilies and water lilies. As he gazed upon it, a thought arose in his mind: "How wonderful it would be if I could possess such a jewel of a woman as this lotus, for she is truly peerless in her grace. Just as this thought occurred to him, a celestial voice resounded from the sky: "O King, you shall indeed obtain that which you desire, provided you remain steadfast in your resolve and do not waver from the path of dharma. Encouraged by these words, the king returned to his palace and summoned his ministers. He told them of his vision and his longing, and they advised him to seek out a wise counselor who might assist him in his quest. Following their counsel, the king appointed a learned Brahmin named Vidyādhara to guide him in this matter. Under the guidance of Vidyādhara, the king set out on a journey to the forest of Gandhamādana, where he encountered a sage named Jñānavatī. The sage, perceiving the king's intention, spoke to him: "O King, the woman you seek is none other than the goddess Lakṣmī herself, who dwells within the depths of the ocean. To attain her, you must perform a great sacrifice and offer up your own life as an oblation. The king, undaunted by the difficulty, agreed to the sage’s proposal. He returned to his kingdom and prepared for the sacrifice. On the appointed day, he entered the sacrificial arena, surrounded by his ministers and priests. As the rites were being performed, the king, true to his word, cast himself into the fire. At that moment, the goddess Lakṣmī appeared before him, radiant and resplendent. She said, "O King, your devotion has been proven. I am pleased with your sacrifice and grant you your wish. You shall possess me as your consort, and your reign shall be prosperous and free from all calamities. Thus, the king attained the fulfillment of his heart's desire, and he and Queen Śrīmatī lived together in happiness, ruling the earth with justice and compassion. And so ends the story of the seventh statuette.

7. The Story of the Seventh Statuette: Two Headless Bodies Brought to Life by Vikrama Southern Recension of 7 The King said: "O Goddess, tell me another story. Sāvitrī replied: "O King, listen. This is the seventh story. Long ago, there was a king named Vikramāditya who ruled over the city of Ujjayinī. Once, while wandering about, he arrived at a certain forest. There, he saw two headless trunks standing upright. Seeing them, the King was struck with wonder and asked his ministers: 'What are these two things? The ministers replied: 'O King, these are two headless trunks that have been brought here by a certain Yakṣa. Then the King said: 'If these two can be restored to life, then I shall give you a reward. Hearing this, the Yakṣa appeared and said: 'O King, if you can restore these two headless trunks to life, then I shall grant you whatever boon you desire. The King agreed. Then the Yakṣa said: 'O King, take these two jars and pour their contents over these two trunks; they will immediately come to life. The King took the jars and poured the water over the trunks. Instantly, the two headless bodies stood up, alive and well. Seeing this miracle, the King was filled with joy. Then the Yakṣa said: 'O King, since you have performed this difficult feat, choose whatever boon you wish from me. The King replied: 'O Yakṣa, if you are pleased with me, then grant me this boon: may I always remain victorious in battle and may my kingdom be free from all calamities. The Yakṣa granted him this boon and vanished. The King returned to his capital, Ujjayinī, and ruled over his subjects with justice and prosperity. Thus ends the seventh story."

8. The Story of the Eighth Statuette (Metrical Recension) The eighth statuette said: "O King, listen to this ancient tale, which is truly a source of great wonder. It concerns a certain king who was devoted to his duty and possessed a mind free from deceit. Once, while that monarch was ruling the earth, a certain Brahmin arrived at his city. He was well-versed in the Vedas, possessed of great learning, and endowed with virtuous conduct. Having approached the king, he spoke these words: 'O King, I am a seeker of knowledge; grant me the means for my livelihood. The king, being compassionate and devoted to dharma, granted him a village as a source of sustenance. Thereafter, the Brahmin lived happily in that village, performing his daily rites. However, due to the power of past karma, he became afflicted by a severe illness. Though treated by physicians and attended by his kin, his condition did not improve. Seeing him thus distressed, his wife spoke to him with tears in her eyes: 'O husband, why do you suffer so? Your body is wasting away. What is the cause of this affliction? Tell me the truth. The Brahmin replied: 'My dear, I have no other ailment than this. It is surely the result of some transgression committed in a former life. His wife then said: 'If it be so, O wise one, tell me what must be done. I shall perform every task required to bring about your recovery. The Brahmin reflected and said: 'O virtuous lady, there is a remedy for this disease, though it is difficult to accomplish. If you can do it, I shall describe it to you. His wife asked: 'What is that difficult task? Speak it to me. I shall certainly carry it out, even at the cost of my own life. The Brahmin said: 'In the city of Ayodhyā, there dwells a king named Sudarśana. He is a performer of sacrifices and a protector of his subjects. Go to him and beg for a single meal. If he grants you that meal, your husband’s illness will be cured. There is no other way to achieve this end. Hearing these words, the woman set out for Ayodhyā. She traveled through many villages and forests until she reached the city. Arriving at the royal palace, she stood before the gatekeeper and spoke: 'O guardian of the gate, inform the king that I, a woman, have come from afar seeking alms. The gatekeeper went inside and reported: 'O King, a woman stands at the gate, desiring to see your majesty. The king, being compassionate, ordered: 'Let her enter. She entered the inner apartments and beheld the king seated upon his throne. Bowing down with humility, she spoke these words: 'O King, I am a woman from a foreign land, come to you for the sake of food. Grant me a single meal, O lord of men. The king, moved by compassion, said: 'O blessed lady, eat as much as you desire. I shall provide you with whatever you need. The woman replied: 'O King, I do not wish for much food. I seek only a single meal, provided that it is given according to the proper rite. The king asked: 'What is the specific manner in which you desire this meal? 1 The first chapter of the *Jñānasiddhi* begins with the homage: "Homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Great Compassionate One. Then, having paid homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the embodiment of the three bodies (*trikāya*), the author sets forth the purpose of the treatise: "In order to explain the supreme accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) through the yoga of the four seals (*mudrācaturyoga*), this *Jñānasiddhi* is composed. Following this, he describes the qualifications of the disciple who is to be initiated into this practice, stating that such a person must possess faith, devotion, and the aspiration for liberation, and be capable of maintaining the commitments (*samaya*). He further explains that the teacher (*ācārya*) must likewise be endowed with the realization of the reality of the Great Seal and be skilled in the methods of initiation and the transmission of the instructions. Thus, the initial section establishes the foundational context of the work by defining its subject matter, purpose, and the necessary prerequisites for both the practitioner and the instructor.

The Story of the Ninth Statuette. When the king asked, "What is this? the statuette said: "O King, listen. This is the story of the ninth statuette. In the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a king named Mahāsena. He was devoted to the welfare of his subjects, possessed of great power, and skilled in the art of governance. His queen was named Śrīmatī, who was endowed with all auspicious marks and was as radiant as the goddess Lakṣmī herself. Now, in that city there was a merchant named Dhanapāla, who was wealthy and renowned for his generosity. He had a daughter named Sūryaprabhā, who was peerless in beauty and possessed of a voice like that of the cuckoo. She was so beautiful that she surpassed even the celestial nymphs in grace. One day, the king, having heard of her fame, summoned her to the palace. Seeing her, he was struck with wonder; her beauty was such that it captivated the hearts of all who beheld her. The king, desiring to marry her, sent messengers to her father, requesting her hand in marriage. Dhanapāla, out of respect for the king, agreed to the proposal. The wedding was celebrated with great splendor, and Sūryaprabhā became the chief queen of King Mahāsena. The king treated her with the utmost affection and honor, and she lived happily in the royal palace. However, because of her extraordinary beauty, many suitors sought her hand from various lands. The king, wishing to test her character and discern her true nature, devised a plan. He summoned a group of handsome young men from different countries and placed them in the women's quarters under the pretext of being attendants. Sūryaprabhā, seeing these men, was filled with curiosity. She began to converse with them, and they, too, were captivated by her charm. As days passed, their intimacy grew, and the king, observing their behavior, became suspicious. One night, while the king was walking about the palace grounds, he overheard the conversation between Sūryaprabhā and one of the young men. They were speaking of their mutual passion and the secrets of their union. Hearing this, the king was deeply troubled. He returned to his chamber, and in the morning, he called together his ministers and counselors to deliberate on what should be done. The ministers advised, "O King, this woman is of ill-repute. She has brought dishonor upon the royal family. It is best that she be banished from the kingdom. But the king, being compassionate and mindful of his past kindness toward her father, could not bring himself to punish her so harshly. Instead, he decided to put her to a test. He summoned a famous courtesan named Manoharā, who was renowned for her wit and skill in seduction. He told her, "Go to Sūryaprabhā and win her over with your charms. If you can make her fall in love with you, I shall grant you great wealth and honor. Manoharā accepted the task and went to the palace. She approached Sūryaprabhā with great courtesy and began to tell her stories of love and passion. Gradually, she won her confidence and gained her favor. One day, when Sūryaprabhā was alone with her, Manoharā said, "O Queen, why do you remain so sorrowful? You are the most beautiful woman in the world, yet you seem to lack joy. Tell me your secret. Sūryaprabhā, moved by her words, confessed her inner turmoil. She spoke of her husband's suspicion and the threat of exile. Manoharā, seizing the opportunity, said, "Do not fear, my lady. I shall help you escape this misery. Come with me, and we shall go to a distant land where no one knows you. With Manoharā’s assistance, Sūryaprabhā fled the palace one night. They traveled far, crossing mountains and rivers, until they reached a dense forest. There, they rested by a clear stream. While they were sleeping, a wild elephant suddenly appeared and attacked them. Sūryaprabhā was trampled and killed, while Manoharā escaped with her life. The king, hearing of her death, was overcome with grief. He performed the funeral rites and mourned her loss for a long time. He realized then that worldly pleasures are fleeting and that attachment leads only to suffering. He turned his mind toward the Dharma and eventually attained liberation. Thus ends the story of the ninth statuette. The moral is this:
