The Story of the Ninth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. His queen was named Śrīmatī, and they had a son named Candraprabha, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, as the prince was strolling through the royal gardens, he encountered a group of ascetics who were practicing severe penances. Seeing their austere lives, he felt a deep sense of compassion and resolved to renounce the world. He returned to his father and said, "O King, I wish to become a wandering mendicant. Please grant me your permission. The king, overcome with grief at the thought of losing his only son, wept bitterly and tried to dissuade him. However, the prince remained firm in his resolve. Finally, the king relented and granted him leave, provided that he would first visit the holy sites and perform acts of charity for the sake of his future welfare. With his father's blessing, Prince Candraprabha set out on a pilgrimage. He visited many sacred places, gave away vast amounts of wealth to the poor, and performed various meritorious deeds. After some time, he arrived at a forest hermitage where he met a wise sage named Jñānavatī. The sage, seeing the prince’s noble character, took him under his care and instructed him in the secrets of spiritual practice. Under his guidance, Candraprabha mastered the arts of meditation and self-restraint. One day, while practicing in solitude, he fell asleep and dreamed of a vision. In the dream, he saw himself ascending a mountain of jewels, where he encountered a radiant figure seated upon a lotus throne. This figure revealed himself to be the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and spoke these words: "O noble youth, you have accumulated great merit through your charity and devotion. Now, listen well: True liberation does not come from mere outward renunciation, but from the purification of the mind. Cultivate loving-kindness (maitrī) toward all beings, for it is the root of all virtue. Be patient in the face of adversity, for patience is the armor of the bodhisattva. And always remain vigilant in your practice, for the path to enlightenment is fraught with obstacles. Upon waking, the prince reflected deeply on the Bodhisattva’s instructions. He realized that true renunciation lay not in abandoning the world, but in transforming the mind. He returned to his father and told him of his dream and his new understanding. The king was filled with joy and praised his son’s wisdom. From that time forward, Prince Candraprabha lived as a lay practitioner, combining worldly duties with spiritual discipline. He governed the kingdom with justice and compassion, and his fame spread far and wide. Eventually, he passed away and was reborn in the realm of Sukhāvatī, where he continued his journey toward Buddhahood. Moral: Even those who possess worldly power can attain spiritual liberation if they cultivate a compassionate heart and follow the teachings of the wise. True renunciation lies in the transformation of the mind, not in the abandonment of external things. Thus ends the story of the Ninth Statuette.

The Story of the Eleventh Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king who ruled over a vast kingdom. He was wise, just, and beloved by his subjects. One day, while wandering through his pleasure gardens, the king encountered a group of ascetics engaged in deep meditation. Intrigued by their serene demeanor, he approached them and asked, "What is the purpose of your ascetic practices? One of the elders replied, "O King, we seek liberation from the cycle of birth and death. We strive to conquer our passions and attain inner peace. The king, impressed by their wisdom, invited them to his palace and offered them great honor and sustenance. However, as time passed, the king became increasingly distracted by the pleasures of his court and neglected his royal duties. His ministers grew concerned and warned him, "Your Majesty, you have abandoned your responsibilities for the sake of these ascetics. This will lead to the ruin of the kingdom. Undeterred, the king continued to spend his days in idle conversation with the ascetics. One evening, as the king lay upon his bed, he heard a voice from the heavens: "O King, if you wish to see the truth of this world, look at the reflection of your own face in the mirror. Startled, the king rose and examined the mirror. To his horror, he saw that his face was aged, wrinkled, and pale—a stark contrast to the vigor he had once possessed. Realizing the fleeting nature of youth and power, he returned to the ascetics and asked for their guidance. They instructed him in the practice of mindfulness and detachment. Under their tutelage, the king renounced his kingdom and became a forest-dweller. He lived a life of simplicity, serving the poor and the sick, and eventually attained a state of profound peace. Thus, the king who once sought worldly pleasures found ultimate fulfillment through the teachings of the ascetics. The moral of the story is that true happiness is found not in material wealth, but in the cultivation of virtue and wisdom. The End.

The Story of the Eleventh Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Campā. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. Now, this king had a daughter named Śrīmatī, who was exceedingly beautiful and virtuous. One day, as the king was seated upon his throne, he heard a voice from the sky proclaiming: "O King, you shall soon behold a maiden of such surpassing beauty that she will eclipse the splendor of all others. Hearing this, the king became filled with curiosity and sent out messengers in all directions to search for such a girl. Meanwhile, in a certain village, there lived a merchant named Dhanapati. He was wealthy and prosperous, possessing many treasures. His wife gave birth to a daughter who was so radiant that her light seemed to illuminate the entire house. She was named Ratnavatī. From the moment she was born, she grew up to be peerless in beauty; her face was like the full moon, her eyes like lotus petals, and her form was as graceful as a goddess. When the king’s messengers arrived in that village, they saw Ratnavatī and were struck with wonder. They reported her beauty to the king, who immediately dispatched a royal messenger to fetch her. When Ratnavatī was brought before the king, he was so captivated by her loveliness that he offered her hand in marriage to his own son, Prince Candraprabha. However, Ratnavatī was not easily won over. She was devoted to her parents and feared the separation from them. She told the king that she would only agree to marry if she could see her father one last time before departing. The king granted her this request, and she returned to her home. There, she took leave of her parents and set out on her journey. As she traveled, she encountered a band of thieves who waylaid her caravan. The thieves seized her and carried her away into the forest. There, they bound her hands and feet and left her in a cave, intending to kill her for her jewels. But Ratnavatī, remaining calm and composed, prayed to the gods for protection. By the power of her virtue, the thieves were overcome by remorse and released her, allowing her to escape. Having escaped the thieves, Ratnavatī continued her journey until she reached a monastery where she found refuge. There, she met a wise monk who instructed her in the dharma and encouraged her to remain steadfast in her faith. After some time, news of her disappearance reached her parents, who were overcome with grief. The king, hearing of this, was deeply distressed and sent out a search party to find his daughter-in-law. Eventually, the search party discovered Ratnavatī at the monastery. She was reunited with her family, and the king, seeing her safety and her unwavering devotion, was filled with joy. He then arranged for her marriage to Prince Candraprabha, and they lived together in happiness. The moral of this story is that virtue and faith are the true ornaments of a person, and that even in times of great adversity, those who remain steadfast in righteousness will find deliverance. Thus ends the eleventh story.

The Story of the Eleventh Statuette Once upon a time, in a certain city, there lived a merchant who was exceedingly wealthy. He possessed vast treasures and many servants, yet he was miserly and lacked compassion. One day, while wandering through the marketplace, he saw a poor man selling wood. Moved by pity, the merchant bought all the wood from him for a high price and gave it to his own servants to carry home. When the servants reached their quarters, they found that the merchant had already distributed the wood among them. Each servant took a portion and went to his own house. However, one particular servant, who was diligent and honest, thought to himself, "This master has shown me great kindness today; I must ensure that he does not suffer for his generosity. With this thought, he returned to the merchant's house and began to pile up the remaining wood in a corner of the courtyard. Meanwhile, the merchant’s wife, who was even more stingy than her husband, became angry when she heard that the wood had been given away. She scolded her husband, saying, "Why have you wasted such a large quantity of wood? You should have sold it for profit! The merchant, however, remained calm and explained the situation. One night, as the merchant lay in bed, he dreamed that a deity appeared before him and said, "O merchant, because you have given wood to those in need, your wealth shall increase tenfold. Furthermore, you shall attain a state of peace and happiness. Upon waking, the merchant felt great joy and resolved to continue his acts of charity. Some time later, the merchant’s fortune indeed increased, and he became even more prosperous. He built a temple and dedicated it to the deity who had appeared in his dream. From then on, he lived a life of virtue, providing for the poor and the needy. Thus ends the story of the eleventh statuette. It teaches that generosity and compassion lead to prosperity and spiritual well-being. *mr, br, jr* (Mūla-ratna-jātaka) Page 104.11. Story of the Eleventh Statuette.

**The Thirteenth Statue: The Story of the King Who Was Devoted to His Subjects** In the city of Śrāvastī there lived a king named Mahāprajāpatī, who was exceedingly devoted to his subjects. He governed with righteousness and provided for the welfare of all beings. One day, as the king was seated upon his throne, he heard a cry of distress from the marketplace. He sent for the wardens and asked, “What is this outcry? They replied, “Your Majesty, a merchant has been robbed by thieves, and his goods have been stolen. The king, filled with compassion, commanded his ministers, “Go quickly and restore the merchant’s property to him. The ministers went out and recovered the stolen goods, returning them to the merchant. Then the king thought to himself, “I must ensure that no one in my kingdom suffers from poverty or injustice. I shall establish a granary where the needy may come and take whatever they require, without asking. Accordingly, he had a great storehouse built and ordered it to be filled with grain, cloth, and other necessities. He proclaimed throughout the city: “Let those who are in need come freely and take what they require; let no one go hungry or destitute in my realm. Thus, under the king’s benevolent rule, the city flourished. The people were contented, and the land was prosperous. The king’s fame spread far and wide, and he became known as the protector of the poor and the defender of the weak. This is the story of the thirteenth statue. It teaches that a ruler who is compassionate and dedicated to the welfare of his subjects will find true happiness and renown. *End of the Thirteenth Story*

The Story of the Thirteenth Statuette Once upon a time, in a certain city, there lived a merchant who was very wealthy and possessed of great merit. He had a son named Sudhana, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, as the merchant was traveling abroad on business, he entrusted his son with the management of the household and the care of his friends and dependents. After some time, the merchant returned home and found that his son had become exceedingly generous and hospitable. He gave away vast sums of wealth to the poor, the needy, and to those seeking refuge, until his entire fortune was nearly exhausted. Seeing this, the merchant’s wife became anxious and said to him, "My lord, your son has squandered our wealth. We must put a stop to this. The merchant replied, "Wife, do not speak thus. My son is practicing the virtue of generosity. It is through such deeds that one attains great merit and happiness in future lives. However, the merchant’s wife remained firm in her opposition. She thought to herself, "If I do not act quickly, we shall be destitute. One night, while the merchant was away, she took a small amount of gold and jewels and fled with her daughter-in-law to another land, leaving Sudhana behind. When the merchant returned and learned what had happened, he was filled with grief and anger. He sent messengers in search of his wife and daughter-in-law, but they could not be found. Meanwhile, Sudhana remained in the house, continuing to give alms to the poor and the destitute. One day, a wandering mendicant arrived at his door. Sudhana welcomed him with joy and offered him food and clothing from the little that remained. The mendicant was deeply moved by his sincerity and told him, "Young man, you possess great merit. By your acts of charity, you have earned a high rebirth. However, you must be careful not to exhaust your resources entirely; for even the most virtuous must maintain their livelihood. Sudhana reflected on these words and realized the wisdom of moderation. From that time forward, he practiced generosity with wisdom, ensuring that his family’s needs were met while still helping others. The story concludes that true virtue lies not in reckless extravagance, but in a balanced life where compassion is tempered by prudence. Thus, the thirteenth statuette teaches that while giving is a noble path, it should be practiced with discernment and care for one’s own well-being.

13. The Story of the Thirteenth Statuette – Brief Recension (BR) Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāprabha who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was endowed with great power and possessed a vast army. His queen was named Śrīmatī, and they had a son named Candraprabha, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. Now, this King Mahāprabha had a minister named Sumati, who was wise, learned, and highly esteemed. One day, as the king sat upon his throne surrounded by his courtiers, he spoke to his minister: "O Minister, tell me of some rare and wonderful thing that has never been seen before. The minister, being a man of great intellect, reflected for a moment and replied: "Your Majesty, there exists a most extraordinary jewel known as the 'Cintāmaṇi' (Wish-fulfilling Gem). It is said that if one possesses it, all desires are fulfilled and no misfortune can ever befall them. The king, hearing this, became filled with longing and commanded his minister to procure such a gem at any cost. The minister, having received the royal command, set out on a journey and traveled through many lands until he reached a distant forest where he encountered a sage. The sage, seeing the minister, asked him the purpose of his journey. The minister related the entire matter to him. The sage, being compassionate, told him: "O noble one, in this very forest dwells a Yakṣa named Manibhadra. He possesses a Cintāmaṇi jewel. If you can obtain it from him, your purpose will be accomplished. Hearing this, the minister was overjoyed and, taking leave of the sage, went to the Yakṣa’s abode. There, he saw the Yakṣa sitting upon a jeweled throne. The minister approached him with humility and requested the Cintāmaṇi. The Yakṣa laughed and said: "O Minister, this jewel cannot be given away so easily. Only one who proves himself worthy may possess it. The minister then challenged the Yakṣa to a test. The Yakṣa agreed and proposed a riddle. He said: "I have three statues made of gold, silver, and iron. Each statue holds a key. The key held by the golden statue opens the door to the silver statue; the key held by the silver statue opens the door to the iron statue; and the key held by the iron statue opens the door to my treasury. You must find the treasury by following these keys. The minister pondered this for a long time. Finally, he realized the solution: the golden statue held the key to the silver statue, the silver statue held the key to the iron statue, and the iron statue held the key to the treasury. Having solved the riddle, he presented the keys in the correct order and opened the treasury. The Yakṣa, pleased with his wisdom, gave him the Cintāmaṇi jewel. The minister took the jewel and returned to the presence of King Mahāprabha. When the king saw the jewel, he was filled with wonder and joy. He honored the minister greatly and bestowed upon him great wealth and rewards. Thus, O King, the minister Sumati, through his intelligence and perseverance, obtained the Cintāmaṇi jewel and brought happiness to his sovereign.
This is the story of the thirteenth statuette.

JR Paragraph: 1 [Translation] In the first chapter of the *Jñānasiddhi*: The venerable Mañjuśrī said: "O Vajrapāṇi, how many types of mantras are there? Vajrapāṇi replied: "O Blessed One, there are three types of mantras. Mañjuśrī asked: "What are those three? Vajrapāṇi replied: "They are the mantra of the Tathāgata, the mantra of the Vidyārāja, and the mantra of the Vajradhara. Mañjuśrī asked: "What is the nature of each of these? Vajrapāṇi replied: "The Tathāgata-mantra is characterized by the nature of the Dharmakāya; the Vidyārāja-mantra is characterized by the nature of the Sambhogakāya; and the Vajradhara-mantra is characterized by the nature of the Nirmāṇakāya. Mañjuśrī asked: "How are these to be applied? Vajrapāṇi replied: "The Tathāgata-mantra is applied for the pacification of all afflictions; the Vidyārāja-mantra is applied for the increase of merit and wisdom; and the Vajradhara-mantra is applied for the subjugation of all obstructive spirits and the accomplishment of all activities. Mañjuśrī asked: "What is the ritual procedure for their recitation? Vajrapāṇi replied: "One should first purify the body through the practice of the threefold cleansing. Then, visualizing oneself as the deity, one should recite the mantra with a mind focused on the syllables, maintaining the proper posture and breath control. For the Tathāgata-mantra, one should employ the mudrā of the lotus; for the Vidyārāja-mantra, the mudrā of the vajra; and for the Vajradhara-mantra, the mudrā of the wheel. Mañjuśrī asked: "What are the signs of success? The Story of the Fourteenth Statuette An Ascetic Warns Vikrama Against Neglect of Royal Duty The King said: "O Sage, tell me how the fourteenth statuette was moved by the power of my merit. The ascetic replied: "O King, listen. Once, while you were wandering through the forest for the sake of hunting, you arrived at a certain hermitage. There, you saw a great sage seated upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, his body emaciated by austerities. Seeing him, you bowed with devotion and sat down before him. Then the sage spoke: 'O King, why have you come here? You who possess the splendor of Indra, it is not fitting for you to abandon the duties of royalty and wander thus in the forest. A king who neglects his royal duties is like a lamp whose oil has been exhausted; he soon perishes. Therefore, O Lord of Men, return to your city and protect your subjects. Hearing these words, O King, you returned to your capital and attended to the affairs of state. The King asked: "O holy one, what fruit did that sage obtain by performing such severe penance? The ascetic replied: "O King, listen. That sage attained the highest state of liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus, O King, even those who practice such rigorous austerities find their goal; how much more so, then, for you, who rule over the earth according to dharma! Thus ends the story of the fourteenth statuette. May you be victorious!

(sr) SR: The fourteenth statuette said: "O King, listen to this story concerning the way in which the wise attain their desired objects through the power of their intelligence. In the city of Pāṭaliputra there lived a merchant named Dhanapāla, who was wealthy and possessed of great fortune. He had a son named Guṇasāgara, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, while wandering about, Guṇasāgara saw a beautiful maiden of noble lineage. Struck by her beauty, he became deeply enamored of her and, unable to bear his passion, he went to his father and said: 'Father, I am in love with that maiden; you must arrange for me to marry her. His father replied: 'My son, she belongs to another family and is not within our reach. However, if you can obtain a certain jewel from the king, I shall fulfill your wish. The son asked: 'Father, what kind of jewel is it? The father said: 'It is a jewel that grants all desires. If you bring it here, I will give you whatever you wish. Guṇasāgara agreed and set out. On the way, he met a wise man who told him: 'Son, do not go to the king’s palace, for the king is difficult to please and full of many traps. Instead, go to the forest where the sage Jñānavatī dwells; she will grant you the jewel. Following his advice, Guṇasāgara went to the forest and found the sage. Bowing down, he related his entire situation. The sage said: 'Young man, I possess a magic spell that enables one to enter the inner apartments of the king. If you apply it, you will see the queen and obtain the jewel. Having received the spell, Guṇasāgara returned to the city and, at night, entered the royal palace by means of the magic power. There he beheld the queen, who was like a goddess, and having gained her favor, he obtained the jewel and departed. He presented the jewel to his father, who was overjoyed and fulfilled his son's desire. Thus, O King, the wise achieve their goals through the application of their intellect. The statuette concluded: "In this way, the wise attain their desired ends through the power of their intelligence. Thus ends the fourteenth story. **The Ascetic Warns Vikrama Against Neglecting Royal Duty** One day, as King Vikrama was seated upon his throne, a certain ascetic approached him. Having prostrated himself before the monarch, he addressed him with these words: "O Great King, you who are the protector of the earth! It is said that the duty of a king is the foremost among all duties. Therefore, you must never neglect the governance of your kingdom. For if a king fails to attend to his royal duties, his subjects fall into distress, and his own merit is diminished. Furthermore, O Lord of Men, it is your responsibility to ensure that the four castes and the four stages of life (*cāturvarṇya-āśrama*) abide by their respective laws. You must uphold justice, protect the weak, and subdue the wicked. Do not allow yourself to be distracted by worldly pleasures or idle pursuits at the expense of your sovereign obligations. Remember, O King, that the prosperity of a realm depends entirely upon the vigilance of its ruler. May you long enjoy the fruits of your righteous reign! Thus admonished, King Vikrama paid due respect to the ascetic and pledged himself to fulfill his kingly duties with unwavering diligence. Thus ends the story of the ascetic’s warning to Vikrama.

15. The Story of the Fifteenth Statuette: The Heavenly Nymph and the Kettle of Boiling Oil Southern Recension of 15 Once upon a time, there lived a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī. He was virtuous, powerful, wealthy, and possessed of great majesty. His realm was free from calamities, and his subjects were contented. Now, it so happened that the king had a daughter who was exceedingly beautiful and endowed with every grace. She was like a goddess descended to earth. Her name was Śrīmatī. One day, as the king sat upon his throne in the assembly hall, surrounded by his ministers, he beheld his daughter seated nearby. Seeing her radiant beauty, he was filled with a deep longing for her to marry a husband worthy of her. "Whom can I find," he thought, "who is of equal lineage, wealth, and virtue, to whom I may give my daughter? Meanwhile, in the city of Rājagṛha, there lived a merchant named Dhanapālita, who was immensely wealthy and highly esteemed. He had a son named Guṇasena, who was handsome, learned, and possessed of great merit. When the merchant heard of King Brahmadatta’s daughter, Śrīmatī, he sent messengers to Vārāṇasī to request her hand in marriage for his son. The king, pleased by the proposal, agreed to the alliance. A grand wedding was prepared, and Guṇasena was brought to Vārāṇasī. There, amidst great festivities, he was united with Śrīmatī. For many years, they lived happily together, enjoying all worldly pleasures. However, as time passed, Guṇasena became weary of the household life. He felt a strong desire to renounce the world and seek liberation. One night, while his wife slept, he rose quietly, took his leave of her, and departed for the forest. His wife, waking up and finding him gone, was overcome with grief and wept bitterly. She searched for him everywhere but could not find him. Eventually, she returned to her father’s house, where she remained in mourning. Meanwhile, Guṇasena entered the forest and met a holy sage. Impressed by the sage’s asceticism, he requested initiation into the religious life. The sage, seeing his sincerity, granted him ordination. Guṇasena practiced meditation with great diligence and soon attained the state of an Arhat, endowed with supernatural powers. News of his attainment reached his former wife, Śrīmatī. Moved by devotion and a desire to see her husband once more, she decided to visit him in the forest. Taking a small vessel of boiled oil, she set out on her journey. As she traveled through the wilderness, she encountered a celestial nymph who had been wandering in search of food. Seeing the woman carrying the vessel of oil, the nymph, driven by hunger, seized the vessel and drank the oil. When Śrīmatī reached the hermitage, she found her husband sitting in meditation. She prostrated herself before him and related her story. Guṇasena, however, remained silent, absorbed in his contemplation. Undeterred, Śrīmatī continued to speak of her love and longing. But the Arhat, unmoved by worldly ties, remained lost in his spiritual state. Finally, the celestial nymph, who had witnessed the entire encounter, appeared before them. She revealed that she was the one who had stolen the oil and explained that she had done so out of necessity. Seeing the power of the Arhat’s discipline and the purity of his heart, the nymph was filled with remorse. She confessed her transgression and begged for forgiveness. Guṇasena, moved by compassion, granted her absolution. Having received his blessing, the nymph returned to her celestial abode, while Śrīmatī remained at the hermitage, filled with joy at having seen her husband once again. Thus, through the power of spiritual practice, even the most difficult obstacles can be overcome.
Thus ends the fifteenth story.

The Story of the Sixteenth Statuette – Brief Recension (BR) The Sixteenth Statuette said: "O King, listen to this story concerning a certain man who, having committed a great sin, was freed from it by means of a small act of merit. The king asked: "What is that story? The statuette replied: "In the city of Pāṭaliputra there lived a merchant named Dhanapāla. He was wealthy, possessed of vast riches, and had many servants. Once, while he was traveling abroad for trade, his wife, a woman of loose conduct, became intimate with a certain servant. As time passed, she conceived a child by him. When her pregnancy reached its full term, she gave birth to a son. Fearing public scandal, she placed the infant in a sealed basket and cast it into the Ganges. Meanwhile, a certain fisherman, while fishing in the river, caught that basket. Opening it, he saw the infant inside, adorned with auspicious marks. Taking him, he brought him home and raised him as his own son, naming him Guṇasāgara. The boy grew up, learned all the arts, and eventually became a skilled sailor. One day, while sailing on the ocean, a great storm arose. The ship was tossed about violently, and the crew cried out in terror. At that moment, Guṇasāgara, moved by compassion, performed an act of truth, saying: 'If I have ever performed even a small act of merit, by that truth may this ship be safe! Immediately, the wind subsided, and the ship reached a peaceful harbor. Upon returning to Pāṭaliputra, Guṇasāgara went to his mother’s house. Seeing her there, he asked: 'Mother, where is my father? She replied: 'Your father died long ago; you were abandoned by me in the river. Hearing this, Guṇasāgara was overcome with grief and set out once more to sea. While at sea, he encountered a ship carrying a great quantity of pearls. The captain, seeing Guṇasāgara’s noble appearance, invited him to share the cargo. On their way back, they were again beset by a fierce storm. The captain prayed to the gods, but to no avail. Guṇasāgara then spoke: 'I am a man of little merit; let me go first so that the rest of the crew may survive. He threw himself overboard. As he fell into the water, he was swallowed by a large fish. The fish was later caught by fishermen and brought to the market. A merchant purchased it, thinking it to be a rare delicacy. When the merchant opened the belly of the fish, he found Guṇasāgara alive. Astonished, he took him home and treated him with great honor. Guṇasāgara then related his entire history to the merchant. The merchant, in turn, told him how his mother had abandoned him. Guṇasāgara, filled with remorse for his past life, resolved to renounce the world. He returned to Pāṭaliputra, sought out his mother, and after reconciling with her, he went to a forest hermitage and became a monk. Through diligent practice, he attained Arhatship. **Jainistic Recension of the Sixteen (JR)** 1. The first is the *Ācārāṅga*, which consists of ten chapters (*adhyayana*). It is the foremost among the scriptures and is the source of all conduct. 2. The second is the *Sūtrakṛtāṅga*, which contains eleven chapters. It is the means for the discernment of the true nature of reality. 3. The third is the *Sthānāṅga*, which consists of ten sections (*sthāna*). It is the treasury of the various categories of the teachings. 4. The fourth is the *Samavāyāṅga*, which contains ten sections. It is the compendium of the concordant doctrines. 5. The fifth is the *Vyākhyāprajñapti* (Bhagavatī), which consists of thirty-six thousand verses. It is the extensive exposition of the questions and answers. 6. The sixth is the *Jñātṛdharmakathā*, which contains twenty-two chapters. It is the narrative of the dharma as known by the Jinas. 7. The seventh is the *Upāsakadaśā*, which consists of ten chapters. The ninth is the *Anuttaraupapātikadaśā*, which consists of ten chapters. It is the description of those who have been reborn in the highest heavens. 10. The fourteenth is the *Anuyogadvāra*, which consists of one chapter. It is the gateway to the systematic exposition of the teachings. 15. The fifteenth is the *Pañcanirgranthī*, which consists of one chapter. It is the treatise concerning the five types of non-attachment. 16. The Story of the Seventeenth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king who possessed a great many elephants. One day, he mounted one of his finest elephants and set out on a journey. As he rode along, he saw a beautiful woman standing by the roadside. She was so radiant and lovely that the king’s heart was immediately captivated. He dismounted from his elephant and approached her. "Who are you? he asked. "Whose daughter are you? And why do you stand here alone? The woman replied, "I am the daughter of a merchant. My father has sent me to fetch water from this well. The king said, "Come with me. You shall be my queen. She consented, and they returned together to the palace. The king installed her as his chief consort, and she lived with him in great happiness. However, the king had another wife, a woman of great jealousy and ill-will. When she learned of the new queen, she became consumed with envy and plotted against her. She spread rumors throughout the court, claiming that the new queen was unfaithful and intended to usurp the throne. The king, though he loved his new wife dearly, began to doubt her. One day, while they were walking in the garden, the king noticed a small statue of a woman carved into a pillar. He asked the new queen, "Do you know who this statue is? She replied, "This is a statue of a virtuous woman who remained faithful to her husband even when he was away for years. Her devotion is such that she has been immortalized in stone. The king thought to himself, "If she is truly virtuous, let us test her. He then ordered his men to place the statue in a secret chamber and to lock it away. He told the queen, "I have placed this statue in a hidden room. If you can identify it by its features alone, I shall grant you a boon. The queen agreed. For several days, she meditated and prayed. Then, one night, she went to the chamber where the statue was kept. By the light of a single lamp, she examined the statue closely. She recognized the woman's face and her posture, and she identified it correctly. The king was amazed and pleased. He granted her a boon, saying, "Ask for anything, and it shall be yours. The queen replied, "I ask only this: that you never again doubt my fidelity. The king agreed, and they lived happily ever after. But the jealous wife, seeing her plot fail, grew even more bitter. She devised a new scheme. She bribed a servant to poison the food of the new queen. When the queen ate, she felt unwell. The king summoned a physician, who diagnosed her condition and prescribed a specific medicine. The jealous wife, hearing of the prescription, stole the medicine and gave it to the king instead. The king took it, thinking it was for the queen. Within hours, he fell gravely ill. The physician was summoned once more, and he realized what had happened. The physician said to the king, "Your majesty, you have taken a poison that will kill you unless you drink the very medicine that would have saved your queen. The king wept and said, "Tell me how I may find it. The physician explained, "The medicine was prepared from a rare herb found only in the mountains. It must be ground by someone who has never looked upon a man other than their own husband. The king sent messengers throughout the land, but no one could be found who fit the description. Finally, they returned empty-handed. Then the king remembered the statue and the queen's virtue. He sent for her. When she arrived, he showed her the medicine. She looked at it and said, "I recognize this medicine. It was prepared by my hand. I prepared it myself to heal you. The king was overcome with emotion. He realized the depth of her love and her purity. He turned to the jealous wife and said, "Because of your malice, you have brought death upon me. You shall be banished from this kingdom forever. Thus, the king was restored to health through the power of the virtuous queen's devotion. And the story of the statue became a testament to the strength of true love and the consequences of jealousy. The Moral: Virtue triumphs over malice, and faithfulness is the foundation of all relationships. Even in the face of adversity, a pure heart remains steadfast. The End. M.R., B.R., J.R. Page 140. *Mahābhārata* Brief Recension of 17 BR: The venerable Vyāsa, having composed this great narrative, taught it to his son Śuka. Then, after the passing of the Kṛta Yuga, when the Tretā Yuga had begun, the sage Lomaharṣaṇa, the son of Sūta, recited this history before the assembly of sages at the Naimiṣa forest during the twelve-year sacrifice of Śaunaka. Having heard this from Lomaharṣaṇa, the son of Sūta, the great sage Vaiśampāyana, who was well-versed in the Vedas, recounted it to Janamejaya, the son of Parikṣit, while he was performing a snake-sacrifice. In this *Mahābhārata*, there are eighteen books (*parvans*), which are as follows: Ādi, Sabhā, Aranya, Virāṭa, Udyoga, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Śalya, Sauptika, Aiṣīka, Strī, Śānti, Anuśāsana, Aśvamedha, Āśramavāsa, Mausala, Mahāprasthānika, and Svargārohaṇa. Within these, there are one hundred thousand verses, which consist of four types of compositions: prose (*gadya*), verse (*padya*), mixed prose and verse (*miśra*), and the *ākhyāna* style. This work is known as the *Jaya*, the *Bhārata*, the *Mahāpurāṇa*, and the *Itihāsa*. It is the source of all other histories and is the supreme means for attaining heaven and liberation. This is the brief summary of the *Mahābhārata*.

18. The Tale of the Eighteenth Statuette: Vikrama Visits the Solar Orb Southern Recension of 18 King Bhoja said: "O wise one, tell me another story. The statuette replied: "Listen, O King. Once, while King Vikramāditya was wandering through the world, he reached the city of Ujjayinī. There, he saw a great temple of the Sun-god. He entered it and beheld a magnificent image of the Sun-god made of gold. Seeing that the deity was not receiving offerings, he thought to himself: 'I shall offer this golden image to the Sun-god. Having resolved thus, he took the image and set out for the solar orb. As he traveled along the path, he met a certain sage who asked him: 'O King, where are you going with this golden image? The king replied: 'I am going to offer this to the Sun-god. The sage said: 'O King, the Sun-god is difficult to approach. He dwells in the midst of a thousand-fold flames. You cannot go there; otherwise, you will surely perish. The king said: 'O holy one, I have come here with the firm resolve to offer this to the Sun-god. I shall not turn back until I have seen him. Having spoken thus, the king proceeded toward the solar orb. As he drew near, he saw the Sun-god seated upon his chariot, surrounded by a host of gods, and shining with a brilliance like ten million fires. Seeing the king approaching, the Sun-god spoke: 'O King, why have you come here? This place is filled with intense heat and is not fit for human beings. Depart at once, lest you meet with destruction. The king replied: 'O Lord of Light, I have come before you with the intent to offer this golden image. I have no other purpose. Grant me your favor. The Sun-god said: 'O King, I am pleased with your devotion. Choose whatever boon you desire from me. The king said: 'O Lord, if you are pleased, grant me this: may my kingdom be free from all calamities, and may I never suffer from hunger or thirst. The Sun-god said: 'So be it. Furthermore, because you have offered this golden image to me, your lineage shall never suffer from poverty, and your descendants shall always be prosperous. Having granted these boons, the Sun-god vanished. King Vikramāditya returned to his own city, Ujjayinī, and ruled the earth with justice and prosperity. Thus ends the eighteenth tale."

The Story of the Eighteenth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king named Śūradatta who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He possessed great power and wealth, yet he was devoid of all virtue. His ministers were likewise wicked, and his subjects lived in constant fear. One day, as the king sat upon his throne in the assembly hall, surrounded by his courtiers, a merchant arrived from a foreign land. He brought with him many rare and precious jewels and presented them to the king. The king, however, being greedy and lacking in discernment, did not value these treasures; instead, he looked with favor upon the low-born attendants who stood nearby. Enraged by this, the merchant thought to himself, "This king is a fool. He does not recognize merit, nor does he appreciate the value of what is truly rare. It would be better for me to go elsewhere. With this thought, he took his goods and departed. Later, a wise man among the king’s subjects approached the monarch and said, "Your Majesty, you have rejected excellent gifts and shown favor to those unworthy. This has caused the merchant to depart, taking with him the wealth that could have benefited the kingdom. The king, hearing this, felt remorse. He realized the error of his ways and resolved to change his conduct. From that time forward, he began to honor the virtuous and treat the wicked with justice. He distributed his wealth generously and governed his people with righteousness. Thus, one should never despise the worthy nor show undue favor to the unworthy, for such behavior leads to the loss of both reputation and prosperity. This is the story of the eighteenth statuette.

The Story of the Eighteenth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. However, he was extremely cruel and given to violence; he took pleasure in inflicting suffering upon others and showed no mercy to anyone. One day, while wandering through the city, the king saw a merchant’s daughter who was exceedingly beautiful. She was like a goddess descended from heaven, with a complexion as fair as the moon and eyes as large as lotus petals. Upon seeing her, the king’s heart was instantly captivated, and he became obsessed with her. He summoned the merchant and demanded that the girl be given to him as his wife. The merchant, fearing for his life and property, agreed to the king’s demand. The king then took the maiden and brought her into his inner apartments. There, he treated her with such cruelty and disregard that she was constantly subjected to physical abuse and mental torment. The girl, however, remained steadfast in her virtue. She maintained a pure heart and never once harbored ill will toward the king, despite his constant mistreatment. One night, as the king lay in bed, he heard a voice speaking from the sky. It said: “O King, you have committed a grave sin by treating this virtuous woman so harshly. Because of this, you shall soon meet with your own destruction. Startled by these words, the king asked his ministers what they thought. They advised him to abandon his cruel ways and treat the merchant’s daughter with kindness and respect. The king followed their counsel; he ceased his abuse and began to honor the girl as his queen. In time, the king’s heart softened, and he became a righteous ruler. He governed his kingdom with justice and compassion, and because of his change of heart, he attained a state of peace and prosperity. Thus, even those who are wicked can be transformed by the power of virtue and patience. This is the story of the eighteenth statuette.

The Story of the Nineteenth Statuette: Vikrama Visits Bali, the King of the Netherworld Once upon a time, King Vikrama was seated upon his throne when a messenger arrived from the netherworld (pātāla). He informed the king that the Lord of the Dead (Yama) had sent him with a message. The messenger said: "O King, the Lord of the Dead has commanded me to say this: 'I have heard that you possess great power and valor. Therefore, come to my realm; I wish to see you. King Vikrama replied: "Messenger, tell the Lord of the Dead this: 'I shall go there only if he can show me the way. Then the messenger returned to the netherworld and reported the king's words to Yama. When the Lord of the Dead heard this, he reflected: "It is not fitting for me to show the path to anyone who comes to me by his own will. However, since he has come as a guest, it would be improper for me to refuse him. Thinking thus, he summoned the Goddess of the Earth (Pṛthivīdevī) and said: "Go to the world of men and bring King Vikrama here. The Goddess of the Earth agreed and departed. She traveled through the three worlds and reached the city of Ujjayinī. There she saw King Vikrama seated upon his throne, surrounded by his ministers. She approached him and spoke: "O King, the Lord of the Dead has sent me to summon you. Please come with me. The king asked: "Goddess, what is the reason for this? She replied: "O King, the Lord of the Dead wishes to see you. It is not right for you to refuse such a request. The king consented and set out with her. As they traveled, the Goddess of the Earth showed him the various wonders of the three worlds. When they reached the netherworld, the Goddess of the Earth vanished. Upon entering the netherworld, King Vikrama beheld a magnificent palace. It was adorned with gold, jewels, and pearls, and filled with celestial maidens. He entered the inner apartments and saw the Lord of the Dead seated upon a throne of precious stones, surrounded by his attendants. The Lord of the Dead rose to greet him and welcomed him with due honor. He offered him a seat and said: "O King, please accept these offerings of hospitality. King Vikrama accepted the offerings and sat down. The Lord of the Dead then said: "O King, I have heard of your fame and your prowess. I have prepared a feast for you; please partake of it. The king replied: "Lord, I am satisfied with the sight of you. I do not require food. The Lord of the Dead insisted: "O King, you must eat; it is my command. The king, desiring to test his resolve, agreed to eat. The Lord of the Dead ordered his servants to serve him a meal of human flesh and blood. As the king began to eat, he felt no revulsion. Instead, he consumed the meal with great relish. When the meal was finished, the Lord of the Dead said: "O King, you have shown great courage. Now, choose a boon. The king replied: "Lord, if you are pleased with me, let me return to my own kingdom in safety. The Lord of the Dead granted his request. The king then departed from the netherworld and returned to Ujjayinī. Upon his arrival, he related his adventures to his ministers and the people. All were amazed by his valor and devotion. Thus ends the nineteenth story of Vikrama’s visit to the netherworld.

The Story of the Nineteenth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king who possessed a great many wives. Among them, one wife was particularly beloved by the king, and she was endowed with every virtue. She was skilled in all the arts, possessed a beautiful form, and was endowed with a sweet voice. One day, while the king was seated on his throne, surrounded by his courtiers, that queen entered the assembly hall. As she approached, her voice was heard from afar, singing a song so melodious that it captivated the hearts of all present. The king, hearing her voice, was filled with joy and called out to her, "Come here! When she arrived before him, the king said, "My dear, you have truly surpassed all others in your skill; your song has brought delight to my heart. The queen replied, "O King, this is not my own talent alone; it is because I am blessed with the grace of the goddess Sarasvatī. The king, desiring to test her further, said, "If this is so, then let us see if you can compose a verse on the spot. The queen agreed and, having reflected for a moment, spoke these verses: "Like the moon amidst the stars, like a lotus in a pond, Like a bee among flowers, so do I stand before you, O King. May your majesty grant me favor, for I am devoted to your service; May your prosperity increase, and may your kingdom be ever secure. The king was greatly pleased and rewarded her handsomely. From that time forward, the queen became known as the "Melodious One," and her fame spread throughout the land. However, there was another wife of the king who was jealous of her. She plotted against the queen, seeking to bring about her downfall. One day, the jealous wife found an opportunity when the queen was away from the palace. She went to the king and whispered in his ear, "O King, that woman is not as virtuous as she claims; she is plotting against your life. The king, though skeptical, could not ignore the words of his favorite wife. He summoned the queen and questioned her, but she remained steadfast and pure. Eventually, the king decided to put her to the test. He commanded that she be placed in a secluded room and provided with only a single drop of oil each day. For many days, the queen lived in that room, subsisting on nothing but the tiny amount of oil. When she emerged, she was radiant and healthy, her beauty undiminished. The king was amazed and asked, "How is it that you remain so strong and beautiful despite such deprivation? The queen replied, "O King, I have learned a secret from the goddess Sarasvatī. By reciting certain mantras and maintaining a pure mind, one can overcome all hardships. This is the power of devotion and spiritual practice. Hearing this, the king’s faith was restored, and he honored the queen even more than before. The jealous wife, seeing her failure, was consumed by shame and remorse. Thus ends the story of the nineteenth statuette. Moral: True virtue and inner strength cannot be destroyed by external trials; rather, they shine all the brighter through adversity. Those who possess wisdom and devotion will always find a way to overcome their difficulties.

The Story of the Nineteenth Statuette – Jr Janistic Recension of 19 Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahābala who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He possessed great power and wealth, and his kingdom was prosperous and free from strife. This king had a son named Śūradatta, who was brave, handsome, and endowed with every virtue. One day, while wandering through the city, Śūradatta saw a beautiful woman. She was so exquisite that she seemed like a goddess descended to earth. Her beauty captivated his heart, and he became consumed by the desire to possess her. He sent messengers to search for her, but they returned empty-handed, unable to find her whereabouts. Distraught by his unrequited love, Śūradatta grew pale and wasted away. His father, King Mahābala, seeing his son’s distress, summoned wise counselors and asked them for advice on how to bring this maiden to him. After much deliberation, the ministers suggested that the king should send out a proclamation throughout the land, offering a great reward to anyone who could provide information regarding the woman’s identity and location. Following their counsel, the king issued a public edict. Meanwhile, the woman had been living in a remote village, having fled from her home out of fear of scandal. One day, she heard of the king’s proclamation and decided to travel to the capital to claim the reward. Upon arriving in Vārāṇasī, she disguised herself as a commoner and went to the palace gate. When the king heard of her arrival, he summoned her to his presence. She entered the royal court and stood before the monarch. The king, recognizing her true beauty despite her disguise, asked her who she was and why she had come. The woman replied, "Your Majesty, I am the daughter of a merchant from the city of Kāśī. My name is Śrīmatī. I have come here to receive the reward you promised for information regarding my identity. The king was astonished by her beauty and grace. He offered her vast wealth, lands, and honors, but she refused them all, saying, "I do not seek riches or status. I have come only because I wish to serve the one who has stolen my heart. She then revealed that it was King Mahābala’s son, Śūradatta, whom she loved. The king, moved by her devotion and the purity of her intent, granted her request. He arranged a grand marriage between Śūradatta and Śrīmatī, and they lived together in happiness, their union blessed by mutual affection and virtue. Thus ends the nineteenth story. It teaches that even when faced with obstacles, a steadfast heart and sincere devotion can overcome all difficulties, leading to a happy conclusion.

The Story of the Twentieth Statuette—Vikrama Visits a Forest Ascetic Once upon a time, King Vikrama traveled through the countryside. While wandering about, he reached a certain forest. There, he beheld a hermit who had renounced all worldly attachments and was dwelling in a state of profound tranquility. The king approached the sage and said, "O holy one, you have abandoned all possessions and live in this forest. What is the purpose of your penance? What is the goal for which you strive? The sage replied, "O King, I am practicing this penance for the sake of attaining liberation. The king asked, "What is the nature of that liberation? The sage answered, "Liberation is the complete cessation of rebirth; it is the state of supreme bliss where there is no further suffering. The king then inquired, "Is such liberation attainable by anyone, or is it difficult to reach? The sage replied, "O King, liberation is indeed difficult to attain. It is not achieved merely by residing in a forest or by outward austerity. Rather, it is attained by one who has conquered the senses, who is free from attachment, and whose mind is fixed on the Supreme Truth. Hearing these words, King Vikrama reflected deeply. He understood that true renunciation lies not in the external abandonment of objects, but in the internal conquest of desire. With this realization, he paid his respects to the sage and departed. Thus ends the twentieth story. May it bring you prosperity.

**The Story of the Twentieth Statuette** Once upon a time, there lived a king named Mahāśakti. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. One day, while he was seated upon his throne, surrounded by his ministers, a messenger arrived from a neighboring kingdom bearing a letter. The messenger presented the letter and said, "Your Majesty, the King of Kalinga has sent this message: 'I have heard that you possess a magnificent elephant named Airāvata. I desire to see it; let it be sent to me immediately. King Mahāśakti read the letter and, feeling insulted, replied with a firm command: "Let the King of Kalinga come to me! I shall not send my elephant to him. The messenger returned to his master and delivered the king's defiant reply. Enraged, the King of Kalinga mobilized his forces and marched against Mahāśakti. A great battle ensued between the two armies. King Mahāśakti fought with valor, but eventually, his troops were defeated, and he was captured along with his elephant, Airāvata. The King of Kalinga took Mahāśakti prisoner and led him into his own city. There, he placed the captive king in a dungeon and seized his elephant. However, as fate would have it, the King of Kalinga soon fell ill and died. His ministers, fearing a rebellion, consulted one another and decided to release Mahāśakti so that he might rule over their kingdom. They brought the captive king out of the dungeon and restored him to his throne. King Mahāśakti regained his kingdom and his elephant, but he remained deeply troubled by the humiliation he had suffered. One night, as he lay awake on his bed, he thought to himself: "What is the use of sovereignty if one must endure such insults? It is better to abandon this life and seek liberation. With this resolve, he renounced the world and became a wandering ascetic. Years passed, and the ascetic Mahāśakti traveled through various lands until he reached a great forest. There, he encountered a sage who was practicing severe austerities. The sage welcomed him and offered him food and shelter. One day, the sage asked Mahāśakti, "O noble one, why have you abandoned your kingdom and become a mendicant? Mahāśakti replied, "O Sage, I have experienced the bitterness of defeat and the pain of captivity. I realized that worldly power is fleeting and fraught with suffering. Therefore, I have sought refuge in the path of spiritual discipline. The sage praised him for his wisdom and told him a story to illustrate the transient nature of fortune. He said: "In ancient times, there was a king named Śibi. He was renowned for his generosity and compassion. One day, a celestial being appeared before him in the form of a pigeon, pursued by a hawk. The pigeon cried out in terror, 'Save me, O King! The hawk demanded the pigeon as his rightful prey. Moved by pity, King Śibi offered to give up his own flesh to save the pigeon. He cut a piece of flesh from his thigh and weighed it against the pigeon in a scale. When the pigeon proved heavier, he cut more flesh from his body. Finally, when he offered his entire body onto the scale, the celestial being revealed his true form and said, 'O King, I am Indra, the Lord of the Gods. I tested you to see the limit of your selflessness. Pleased with his virtue, Indra granted him a boon. Śibi chose the boon of eternal righteousness and the protection of all living beings. Upon hearing this, King Mahāśakti was filled with joy. He understood that true greatness lies not in worldly power, but in the purity of one's heart and the practice of virtue. Having gained this insight, he continued his ascetic life with renewed vigor, eventually attaining liberation. Thus ends the story of the twentieth statuette. It teaches that even those of great power must face the vicissitudes of fortune, and that the pursuit of spiritual truth is superior to the pursuit of worldly dominion.

**The Story of the Twentieth Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king who possessed great wealth and power. He had a son who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. However, the prince was deeply addicted to the vice of hunting. Day after day he would go out into the forest with his retinue, leaving the affairs of state to his ministers. One day, while the prince was away on a hunt, a messenger arrived from the city to inform him that the kingdom was in danger of being seized by a neighboring enemy king. The messenger pleaded with him to return immediately to protect his realm. The prince, however, paid no heed to the warning; instead, he continued his pursuit of wild animals. As he roamed deeper into the forest, the prince became separated from his party. As night fell, he found himself alone and lost. Exhausted and terrified, he wandered until he came across a small hut in the middle of the woods. Inside sat an old woman who offered him food and shelter for the night. She told him that she lived there alone and that the forest was filled with many dangers. The prince, weary and hungry, accepted her hospitality. As they conversed, the old woman asked him about his lineage and his travels. When she learned of his royal birth and his current predicament, she felt compassion for him. "My dear youth," she said, "this forest is not safe for you. Tomorrow morning, when you leave, take this small statue of a deity. It possesses a miraculous power; if you carry it with you, no harm shall come to you. The next morning, the prince took his leave and set out toward the city. As he traveled, he encountered various obstacles—wild beasts, treacherous paths, and hostile bandits—but by the power of the statue, he passed through them all unharmed. Finally, he reached the outskirts of the capital. There, he saw his army preparing for battle against the enemy forces. Upon seeing his son return safely, the king was overjoyed. He welcomed him back and took charge of the kingdom once more. The prince, having been saved by the miraculous statue, resolved to abandon his vices and rule the land with justice and wisdom. Thus, the twentieth statuette teaches that even those who are lost in the wilderness of worldly distractions can find their way home through the grace of virtue and the protection of the divine. *End of the Twentieth Story*

**The Story of the Twentieth Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Pāṭaliputra. He was a man of great power and possessed of immense wealth; however, he was utterly devoid of virtue and lacked all moral conduct. One day, while wandering through the city, he saw a certain Brahmin who was exceedingly handsome and well-versed in the Vedas. Seeing him, the king summoned him and said, "O Brahmin, I desire to marry your daughter. The Brahmin replied, "O King, I have only one daughter, and she is already betrothed to another. Therefore, I cannot grant your request. The king, being stubborn and driven by lust, insisted repeatedly until the Brahmin, out of fear of the royal power, finally agreed. He brought his daughter before the king, and the king married her with great pomp and ceremony. After some time, the king took the Brahmin’s daughter as his chief queen and began to enjoy himself with her. However, because the woman was of low birth, the king's other wives could not tolerate her presence. They conspired together and began to plot against her. One day, the king went on a hunting expedition. While he was away, the other queens gathered around the Brahmin’s wife and said, "We have heard that you are the daughter of a low-caste woman. If the king learns of this, he will surely abandon you and even punish us. Therefore, we must find a way to prove your noble lineage. They then devised a plan. They took a young girl from a family of high caste and dressed her in the clothes of the Brahmin’s wife. When the king returned from the hunt, they presented the girl to him, claiming, "This is the Brahmin’s daughter whom you married. The king, seeing the girl’s noble appearance and hearing their words, believed them. He then ordered the Brahmin’s wife to be cast into a dark dungeon and left there alone. Meanwhile, the Brahmin’s wife, though confined in the dungeon, remained faithful to her husband and maintained her purity. She prayed daily to the gods for deliverance. One night, a divine being appeared to her in a dream and said, "Do not despair. Your virtue shall be vindicated. Tomorrow, when the king comes to visit you in the dungeon, he will see a golden image of a goddess upon your head. At that sight, his doubts will vanish and he will restore you to his favor. The next morning, the king visited the dungeon as he had promised. To his amazement, he saw the golden image upon the Brahmin’s wife’s head. Struck with wonder and realizing his error, he fell at her feet in repentance. He released her from the dungeon, restored her to his position as queen, and treated her with great respect. From that time forward, the king lived righteously and governed his kingdom with justice. The story of the Brahmin’s wife became famous throughout the land, and it served as a lesson that virtue is never lost, no matter how great the adversity. Thus ends the twentieth story.

He was a righteous ruler who governed his kingdom with justice and compassion. However, he had no son to carry on his lineage. One day, as the king sat upon his throne, a celestial voice spoke from the sky: "O King, if you wish for a son, you must perform a great sacrifice and offer your own flesh as an oblation. Hearing these words, the king was filled with joy. He summoned his ministers and priests and consulted them regarding the matter. They advised him that such a sacrifice would indeed grant him a son, but it would require the king to offer his own body. Undeterred by the difficulty, the king resolved to fulfill his duty. He prepared for the sacrifice, and on an auspicious day, he ascended the sacrificial altar. As he was about to cut off his own flesh, a divine being appeared before him and said, "O King, do not harm yourself! I am pleased with your devotion and self-sacrifice. I shall grant you a son who will be wise, powerful, and a protector of the Dharma. With these words, the divine being vanished, and the king returned to his palace. Not long after, the queen conceived, and in due time, she gave birth to a son of extraordinary beauty and virtue. The child was named Mahāprabha. As Mahāprabha grew, he became renowned for his wisdom, generosity, and compassion. He studied all the sciences and mastered the arts of governance. One day, while wandering through the city, he encountered a poor man suffering from hunger and thirst. Moved by pity, the prince offered him food and drink from his own storehouse. Later, the prince heard of a sage living in the forest who possessed profound knowledge of the Dharma. He went to visit the sage and requested instruction. The sage taught him the nature of impermanence, the suffering inherent in worldly existence, and the path to liberation. Having gained deep insight into the truth, Prince Mahāprabha renounced his royal status and became a monk. He practiced meditation with great diligence and eventually attained enlightenment. He returned to his father’s kingdom to teach the Dharma to his people, leading them away from suffering toward the bliss of Nirvāṇa. Thus ends the story of the twenty-first statuette. It teaches that true greatness lies not in worldly power, but in wisdom, compassion, and the pursuit of spiritual liberation. Even a king, through self-sacrifice and devotion, can attain a son who brings light to the world and leads others to the truth.

**The Story of the Twenty-First Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king who ruled over a vast kingdom. He possessed great wealth and power, yet he was deeply troubled by his lack of a son. Desiring an heir to the throne, he consulted with astrologers and Brahmins, who advised him that his wish would be fulfilled if he performed a great sacrifice. Following their instructions, the king prepared for the ritual. He gathered all the necessary materials and invited priests of great learning and virtue to conduct the ceremony. On the appointed day, the sacrifice commenced amidst great pomp and splendor. As the rites were being performed, the king’s queen, filled with hope, entered the sacrificial chamber. Suddenly, a miraculous event occurred. From the midst of the flames, a beautiful child emerged, radiant and divine. The priests and the courtiers were filled with wonder and joy. The king took the child in his arms and named him Prince Candraprabha. As the years passed, Prince Candraprabha grew into a handsome and virtuous youth. He was well-versed in the arts of war and peace, and he became beloved by all his subjects. One day, as the prince was strolling through the royal gardens, he encountered a group of merchants returning from a distant land. They told him of a magnificent city called Ratnadvīpa, where the people lived in prosperity and happiness. Filled with curiosity, the prince decided to visit this wondrous place. Accompanied by a small retinue, he embarked on a long journey. After many days of travel, he arrived at the outskirts of Ratnadvīpa. There, he met an old sage who lived in solitude. The sage welcomed the prince and offered him hospitality. Over the course of their conversation, the sage revealed a profound secret. He told the prince that in Ratnadvīpa, there lived a princess named Śrīmatī, who was destined to be his wife. However, the sage warned him that she was guarded by a fierce demoness who would stop at nothing to prevent her union with a mortal. Undaunted, the prince resolved to find Śrīmatī. With the sage’s guidance, he entered the city and searched for her. Finally, he found her in a secluded grove, surrounded by her handmaidens. She was indeed as beautiful as the sage had described. The prince approached her, and they fell in love at first sight. However, the demoness soon discovered their meeting. Enraged, she pursued them, threatening to destroy the prince. Undeterred, Candraprabha confronted her. Through his courage and wisdom, he outwitted the demoness and freed Śrīmatī. Together, they returned to their kingdom, where they were welcomed with great joy. Prince Candraprabha and Princess Śrīmatī lived happily ever after, ruling the kingdom with justice and compassion, fulfilling the king’s greatest desire. Thus ends the story of the twenty-first statuette.

**The Story of the Twenty-Second Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a righteous ruler who governed his kingdom with justice and compassion. However, he had no son to carry on his lineage. One day, the king went to the forest to hunt. While wandering through the woods, he came across a beautiful hermitage belonging to a great sage named Kaśyapa. The sage welcomed the king with hospitality and offered him food and water. As they sat together, the king expressed his sorrow regarding his childlessness. The sage, possessing great wisdom, replied, "O King, if you desire a son, you must perform a great sacrifice to the gods. Only then will your wish be fulfilled. The king returned to his capital and prepared for the sacrifice. He gathered all the necessary materials and invited priests to conduct the ritual. On the appointed day, the sacrifice began. As the fire blazed and the offerings were made, a divine voice resounded from the heavens, declaring that the king would soon have a son who would be a great hero and a protector of the earth. Filled with joy, the king returned home. In due time, his queen gave birth to a son of extraordinary beauty and strength. The boy was named Mahābala. As he grew up, he became a master of all martial arts and sciences. One day, while out hunting, Mahābala encountered a fierce tiger that was threatening a deer. Without hesitation, the prince slew the tiger with a single arrow. The deer, grateful for its life, followed the prince back to the palace and told the story of his deliverance. The king was overjoyed at his son's valor and rewarded the deer with gifts. From that day forward, the deer became a constant companion to Mahābala, following him wherever he went. Years passed, and the king decided it was time for his son to take charge of the kingdom. He summoned Mahābala and said, "My son, you are now capable of ruling this vast empire. I shall retire to the forest to seek spiritual liberation. Mahābala bowed before his father and accepted the responsibility. He ruled with justice and kindness, and his reign was marked by peace and prosperity. One day, as Mahābala was sitting in his palace garden, the deer approached him. The prince stroked the animal affectionately and asked, "Friend, what do you wish for? The deer replied, "O Prince, I am old and weary. I wish to go to the forest to die in peace. The prince was moved by the deer's request. He led the deer to the edge of the forest and set him free. The deer bounded away into the wilds, never to return. The prince wept at the loss of his loyal friend. He realized that even animals could feel gratitude and friendship. He reflected deeply on the transient nature of life and the importance of compassion. From that moment on, Mahābala devoted himself to acts of charity and virtue. He built hospitals for the sick, dug wells for the thirsty, and established schools for the ignorant. His fame spread far and wide, and people from all lands came to seek his counsel and protection. When the king Mahāsena passed away, Mahābala ascended the throne. Under his rule, the kingdom flourished more than ever before. He proved that true greatness lies not in power or wealth, but in the heart of compassion and the deeds of righteousness. Thus ends the story of the twenty-second statuette. It teaches us that even a small act of kindness can lead to great rewards, and that true leadership is rooted in love and service to others. *SR Page: 168* *22. **The Story of the Twenty-Second Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāśakti who ruled over the city of Śrāvastī. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. One day, while wandering through his pleasure gardens, he encountered a young woman of extraordinary beauty. She was so radiant that she seemed to outshine the very flowers of the springtime. Captivated by her splendor, the king summoned her to his palace. There, he took her as his queen, and they lived together in great happiness. However, as time passed, the king became suspicious of her character and feared that she might plot against him. To test her, he devised a cruel plan. He ordered a large iron cauldron to be heated until it was glowing red-hot. Then, he commanded his guards to place the queen inside the vessel and seal it shut. The king himself watched from a distance, his heart heavy with dread. After some time, the guards returned to report that the queen had emerged from the cauldron unscathed, her beauty even more radiant than before. The king was filled with wonder and asked how this could be. The queen replied, "Your Majesty, I have no power to save myself. It was the power of a certain holy man who lives in the forest nearby. The king, eager to see this miracle for himself, set out for the forest. There he found the sage, a man of great asceticism and spiritual power. The king prostrated before him and explained his situation. The sage, moved by compassion, granted the king a boon. The king requested that he be shown the way to attain such power as to never again suffer harm. The sage instructed him in the practice of the *Dharmapāla* mantra and taught him the ritual for its recitation. The king returned to his palace and began to perform the rites with unwavering devotion. Meanwhile, the queen, having witnessed the king's newfound faith, felt a deep sense of remorse for her past suspicions. She too began to practice the mantra with sincerity. One night, while the king was asleep, the queen saw a vision in which the *Dharmapāla* appeared and spoke to her, saying, "Fear not, O Queen; you shall be protected by my power. From that day forward, the king and queen lived in peace and prosperity, their hearts united in faith. The story of their deliverance spread throughout the land, and many others followed their example in honoring the *Dharmapālas*. Thus ends the twenty-second story. It teaches that even those who have committed grave errors may find redemption through sincere devotion and the grace of the protectors of the Dharma. One should never underestimate the power of truth and virtue.

The Story of the Twenty-third Statuette: Vikrama’s Daily Life; His Evil Dream Vikrama sat upon his throne, surrounded by his ministers. As he was seated there, the chief minister spoke: "O King, it is time for you to retire to your private chambers. The king replied: "I have not yet finished my daily duties. First, let me hear the report of the spies regarding the affairs of the city and the countryside. The minister said: "O King, the reports of the spies have already been heard. Now, please proceed with your evening routine. The king then asked: "What is the news from the city? Is all well with the people? The minister replied: "O King, all is well. However, there is one matter that must be reported. A certain merchant named Dhanadatta has died. He was a man of great wealth, but he left no son. Therefore, his vast fortune will now pass to the royal treasury. Hearing this, the king reflected: "Alas! Wealth is indeed transient. It is like a drop of dew upon a blade of grass. One moment it is abundant, and the next it vanishes. I too am subject to the same law of impermanence. Just as he was pondering these thoughts, a messenger arrived and announced: "O King, a terrible dream has occurred to Your Majesty. Last night, you saw yourself falling from a mountain peak into a vast ocean of fire. You were consumed by flames, yet you did not perish. This dream is most ominous. The king, hearing this, became deeply distressed. He summoned his court astrologers and asked them to interpret the dream. They consulted their scriptures and replied: "O King, this dream portends great danger. It foretells that some calamity shall soon befall you. To avert this misfortune, you must perform a great sacrifice and offer gifts to the Brahmins. The king, though troubled, remained resolute. He said: "If fate has ordained this, I shall face it with courage. Let the rites be performed, and let my subjects be protected. Thus, the king attended to his daily affairs, undaunted by the omen. But the shadow of anxiety lingered over him, like a dark cloud hovering at the edge of the horizon.

The Story of the Twenty-third Statuette Once upon a time, in a certain city, there lived a merchant who was extremely wealthy. He possessed vast riches and a great many servants. Now, this merchant had a son named Sudhana, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, as the merchant was sitting on his veranda, he saw a group of young women passing by. They were adorned with fine garments and ornaments, and they moved with graceful steps. Seeing them, the merchant’s son felt a deep longing arise within him. He asked his father, "Father, who are these women? Whose daughters are they? The merchant replied, "My son, those are the daughters of a neighboring merchant. They are renowned for their beauty and virtue. Sudhana said, "Father, I wish to marry one of them. The merchant consented, saying, "Very well, my son. I shall arrange it. He then sent messengers to the other merchant’s house, and after much negotiation, the two families agreed to the marriage. A grand wedding was prepared, and Sudhana was married to the daughter of the merchant. After some time, the merchant fell ill. Knowing that his end was near, he called his son Sudhana to him and said, "My son, I have accumulated great wealth through my business. I wish to entrust it all to you, so that it may continue to benefit our family. Sudhana replied, "Father, I am grateful for your kindness. However, I do not wish to take charge of such vast wealth. I wish instead to go abroad and seek my own fortune through trade. The merchant, seeing that his son was firm in his resolve, gave him his blessing and permitted him to depart. Sudhana took leave of his parents and set out on his journey. After traveling for many days, he arrived at a great city. There, he found a wise old man who was a master of astrology and divination. Sudhana approached him and said, "O wise one, please tell me where I might find great wealth and success. The old man examined Sudhana’s palm and face and said, "Young man, you possess the marks of prosperity. If you travel toward the south, you will encounter a great ocean. There, you will find a ship laden with precious jewels. By acquiring these, you will achieve your goal. Encouraged by these words, Sudhana traveled south until he reached the shore of the great ocean. He hired a merchant vessel and embarked upon the sea. After many days at sea, the ship encountered a fierce storm. The waves rose high, and the crew was terrified. Sudhana prayed fervently to the gods and goddesses, and by the power of his devotion, the storm subsided. The ship continued its course safely until it reached a distant island. On the island, Sudhana discovered a cave filled with gold, silver, pearls, and other precious gems. He collected a vast amount of treasure and returned to his ship. Upon reaching his home city, Sudhana presented the wealth to his father. His father was overjoyed and praised his son’s wisdom and courage. Sudhana lived happily ever after, enjoying the fruits of his endeavors. Thus ends the story of the twenty-third statuette.
