1 The first section of the *Jñānasiddhi* (JR) begins with an homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the embodiment of the three bodies (*trikāya*). It then proceeds to explain that the ultimate reality (*tattva*) is the non-dual nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is free from all conceptual elaborations (*prapañca*). This reality is characterized by the union of bliss (*sukha*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and it is the very essence of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). The text further establishes that this state is not something to be newly produced, but is rather the primordial nature of all phenomena, which is realized through the purification of the habitual tendencies of dualistic grasping. Thus, the path consists of the integration of method (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), leading to the direct perception of the innate mind (*cittaprakṛti*).

The Story of the Twenty-Fourth Statuette: A Strange Inheritance—Śālivāhana and Vikrama The twenty-fourth statuette said: "O King, listen to this story concerning a most extraordinary inheritance involving Śālivāhana and Vikrama. In the city of Pratishthāna there lived a king named Śālivāhana. He was a man of great power, possessing a vast army and abundant wealth. One day, while wandering through the forest for sport, he encountered a sage who had attained supernatural powers. The sage, seeing the king, spoke to him: "O King, you are a man of great merit; therefore, I shall grant you a boon. The king replied, "O Holy One, if you are pleased with me, then grant me the boon that I may possess inexhaustible wealth and an army that is never defeated in battle. The sage said, "So be it," and bestowed upon the king a miraculous vessel from which all manner of riches could be drawn at will. Furthermore, he granted him a sword that was invincible in combat. Having received these gifts, King Śālivāhana returned to his capital, where he ruled with great prosperity. Now, in the city of Ujjayinī, there reigned a king named Vikrama. He was a man of great valor, devoted to justice, and beloved by his subjects. One day, as he was walking through the city, he heard a cry of distress from a merchant's son who was being pursued by a group of thieves. The Story of the Twenty-fourth Statuette – Metrical Recension of 24 Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahābala who ruled over the city of Śrāvastī. He was a sovereign endowed with great power and majesty, and his kingdom was prosperous and free from all calamities. Now, it so happened that this king had a daughter named Candraprabhā, who was as radiant as the moon and possessed of every auspicious mark. She was skilled in all the arts and sciences, and her beauty was such that she surpassed even the celestial nymphs. One day, while wandering through the pleasure gardens, the princess beheld a young man of extraordinary appearance. He was like a god descended to earth, his form adorned with the marks of a great being. Struck by his splendor, she felt an immediate and profound affection for him. The youth, for his part, was also captivated by her beauty and grace. They met in secret, and their love grew deep and tender. However, the king, learning of their attachment, became enraged. Thinking that the youth was unworthy of his daughter’s hand, he ordered his ministers to have him executed. The ministers, though fearful of the king’s wrath, could not bring themselves to carry out the order against one so virtuous. They concealed the youth and brought him before the princess, saying, "He has been punished by the king. Candraprabhā, hearing this, was overcome with grief. She resolved to follow him in death, for she could not bear to live without her beloved. With the permission of her parents, she prepared herself for the journey. Meanwhile, the youth, having escaped the executioners, fled to a distant forest. There, he encountered a sage who instructed him in the ways of dharma and self-restraint. Through the sage’s guidance, he attained spiritual insight and became a holy man. Candraprabhā, meanwhile, accompanied by her maidens, traveled to the forest. There, she found her husband transformed by asceticism. Recognizing him by his divine radiance, she prostrated herself at his feet. The youth, moved by her devotion, revealed his true nature and recounted his trials. He told her how he had renounced worldly life to seek liberation and how he had found peace through the teachings of the sage. Filled with joy, the princess embraced her husband and vowed to follow his path. Together, they lived in the forest, practicing virtue and compassion, until they both attained the highest state of bliss. Thus ends the twenty-fourth story. It teaches that true love transcends worldly obstacles and that devotion to dharma leads to ultimate fulfillment.
One should always honor those who possess wisdom and virtue, for they are the true ornaments of the world.

**The Twenty-Fifth Statuette: The Story of the Twenty-Fifth** Once upon a time, there was a king named Śūradatta who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power, possessed of immense wealth and vast armies. His kingdom was prosperous, free from strife, and filled with abundant harvests. Now, this King Śūradatta had a son named Mahāśūradatta. The prince was handsome, endowed with all auspicious marks, and skilled in every branch of learning. However, he was deeply addicted to the vice of hunting. Day after day, he would go out into the forest with his retinue of hunters, slaying deer, wild boars, and other forest creatures. One day, while the prince was wandering through the dense woods, he came across a hermitage belonging to a group of sages. There, he beheld a young maiden of extraordinary beauty, the daughter of the sage. She was radiant as a goddess, adorned with the splendor of asceticism. Struck by her beauty, the prince’s heart was captivated. Approaching the hermitage, the prince asked the sage for the hand of his daughter in marriage. The sage, observing the prince’s noble lineage and his devotion, consented to the union. The prince took the maiden home and lived with her in great happiness. However, the prince’s addiction to hunting did not diminish. Despite the presence of his beloved wife, he continued to frequent the forests, neglecting his royal duties. Consequently, the kingdom began to decline; the people suffered, and the enemy kings saw their opportunity. One day, while the prince was away on a hunt, the enemy forces invaded the city. They captured the king, his ministers, and the citizens, and laid siege to the palace. When the prince returned, he found his capital in ruins and his father imprisoned. Filled with remorse, the prince vowed to restore his father’s honor. He gathered his remaining troops and set out to wage war against the invaders. In the midst of the battle, the prince displayed such valor that he single-handedly routed the enemy army. He rescued his father and reinstated him upon the throne. Having fulfilled his duty and restored peace to the land, the prince turned his mind toward spiritual matters. He realized that worldly pleasures were fleeting and that true happiness lay in renunciation. He entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and retired to the forest to live as an ascetic. Thus ends the twenty-fifth story. It teaches that even those of noble birth must conquer their vices, for only through self-restraint and virtue can one achieve lasting peace and honor.

Vikrama Averts an Astrological Evil Omen (Southern Recension 25) Once, while King Vikramāditya was seated upon his throne, the royal astrologer announced: "O Great King, an evil planetary conjunction has occurred; it portends a great calamity for Your Majesty. The king replied: "If such is the case, what must be done? The astrologer said: "O King, there is no remedy other than the gift of one's own head. Hearing this, the king summoned his ministers and said: "If my life is to be lost, let it be so; I shall not abandon righteousness. Therefore, let a man who is willing to give his own head be sought out. At that time, there lived a certain merchant named Dhanapati. He had a son named Guṇākara, who was devoted to virtue and possessed of great compassion. One day, he went to the marketplace to sell various goods. While wandering about, he heard the king’s proclamation regarding the gift of a head. Upon hearing this, Guṇākara thought: "What greater merit could there be than to save the life of a king through the sacrifice of my own head? It is better to die now than to live a life devoid of dharma. With this resolve, he went to the palace and informed the gatekeeper: "I am a man who is ready to give his own head. The gatekeeper, filled with wonder, reported this to the king. The king summoned him and asked: "Are you truly prepared to give your own head? Guṇākara replied: "O King, I am indeed prepared to give my head for the sake of dharma. The king said: "If this is so, then come tomorrow morning; I shall perform the ritual of offering my own head. Guṇākara returned home and told his parents: "Father and Mother, I have resolved to give my head for the sake of dharma. Grant me your permission. His parents, overcome with grief, said: "Son, why do you speak such words? We have no wealth, nor do we possess even a single coin. How can we provide for your funeral rites? Furthermore, who will take care of us when you are gone? Do not go; rather, remain here and serve the king. Guṇākara said: "Father and Mother, I have no desire for wealth or worldly pleasures. I wish only to attain the imperishable state. If you grant me permission, I shall depart; if not, I shall fast unto death. Seeing his firm resolve, his parents granted him leave, saying: "Go, my son, may you attain success. Then Guṇākara went to the palace and stood before the king. The king, having performed the auspicious rites, sat upon a high seat and prepared to offer his own head. At that moment, Guṇākara stepped forward and said: "O King, please grant me your permission; I shall offer my own head. The king was astonished and said: "O noble one, why do you speak thus? You are young and full of vigor; you should enjoy the pleasures of life. Leave this matter to me. Guṇākara replied: "O King, I have no attachment to the body, which is as transient as a bubble. I seek only the eternal dharma. Therefore, please permit me. The king, seeing his unwavering devotion, praised him and said: "O virtuous one, you are truly a jewel among men. Since you are so resolute, I shall grant your wish. Then, with great solemnity, the king placed Guṇākara upon the sacrificial altar and prepared to strike his head with a sword. Just as the blow was about to fall, the king suddenly felt a divine touch and awoke from his dream-like trance. He saw that it was all but a vision, and he realized that his own head had not been severed. Overjoyed, the king embraced Guṇākara and said: "O blessed one, by your grace my life has been saved. Ask for any boon you desire, and I shall grant it. Guṇākara replied: "O King, if you are pleased with me, then let this kingdom be free from fear and calamity. Let no evil omen ever again afflict Your Majesty. The king agreed to this and honored Guṇākara with great wealth and respect. From that day forth, the kingdom remained peaceful, and the evil planetary influence was averted. Thus, King Vikramāditya, through his own courage and the devotion of a virtuous subject, overcame a grave astrological misfortune.

**The Story of the Twenty-Fifth Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsena who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast army. However, he was deeply troubled by the thought that his kingdom was not secure from the threat of enemies. One day, while wandering through the city, the king came across a wise man who was renowned for his knowledge of statecraft. The king approached him and asked, "O wise one, how can I ensure that my kingdom remains free from the fear of enemies? The wise man replied, "Your Majesty, the security of a kingdom depends upon the strength of its defenses. Therefore, you should build a fortress that is impregnable. Following this advice, the king ordered the construction of a magnificent fortress on a high mountain peak. It was built with walls of solid stone and equipped with towers and battlements. Once completed, the king took up residence within it and lived there for many years, free from all anxiety. However, after some time, the king became weary of living in such isolation. He longed to see the world outside once more. One day, he summoned his ministers and said, "I wish to travel abroad and see the lands of other kings. Prepare a chariot for me. The ministers prepared a grand chariot and presented it to the king. The king mounted the chariot and set out on his journey. As he traveled, he encountered various kingdoms, each more prosperous than the last. He saw cities filled with wealth, people enjoying themselves, and rulers who were powerful and respected. Upon returning to his own kingdom, the king reflected on what he had seen. He thought to himself, "My own kingdom is indeed prosperous, yet it lacks the splendor of these other realms. I must strive to improve it further. With this thought in mind, the king began to administer his realm with even greater diligence. He encouraged agriculture, promoted trade, and ensured that justice was served fairly. Under his rule, the kingdom flourished, and the people lived in peace and abundance. Years passed, and the king’s reign became celebrated throughout the land. His enemies, hearing of his virtues and the prosperity of his realm, ceased their hostilities and sought instead to form alliances with him. Thus, the king achieved the very security he had once feared. When the king grew old, he entrusted the kingdom to his son and retired to the forest to live as a hermit. There, he spent his remaining days in meditation and reflection on the nature of worldly existence. The moral of this story is that true security comes not merely from physical defenses, but from the wisdom and virtue of the ruler. A kingdom prospers when its leader acts with justice and foresight, ensuring the well-being of both his subjects and his enemies alike. Thus ends the twenty-fifth story.

The Story of the Twenty-Sixth Statuette Once upon a time, there lived a king named Mahāsena. He was a man of great power and possessed a vast kingdom. However, he was devoid of all virtue and was addicted to every vice. His conduct was such that he caused suffering to his subjects and brought misery upon the world. One day, while wandering through the city, the king came across a woman who was exceedingly beautiful. Her form was like that of a goddess, and her grace surpassed even the celestial nymphs. Seeing her, the king’s heart was instantly captivated by passion. He summoned her to his palace and made her his queen. The king then gave orders to his ministers, saying, "I wish to conquer the entire earth. Prepare my army and set out at once. Having received these commands, the ministers gathered a vast host of soldiers and marched forth. As they traveled, they encountered a great sage who was seated beneath a tree, absorbed in meditation. The king approached him and asked, "O holy one, where is the path that leads to the conquest of the whole earth? The sage replied, "O King, the conquest of the earth lies in the direction where the sun rises. Go there and you shall achieve your desire. Following the sage's instruction, the king proceeded toward the eastern quarter. On his way, he came upon a forest where he saw a magnificent temple dedicated to Śiva. Inside the temple stood a statue of the Lord, carved from a single block of precious stone. It was so exquisitely crafted that it seemed as if the deity himself were present. Seeing this, the king was filled with wonder. He entered the temple and began to worship the Lord with great devotion. As he offered his prayers, a voice resounded from within the shrine: "O King, if you truly desire to conquer the earth, you must first offer this very statue as a sacrifice to me. Startled by these words, the king consulted his ministers. They advised him, "O King, this is a divine command. To achieve your goal, you must not hesitate. Offer the statue as an oblation, and you shall surely gain victory over the world. Though his heart was heavy with grief, the king agreed to their counsel. He ordered his men to prepare the sacrificial altar and to bring the statue forward. As the ritual was being performed, the statue suddenly vanished, leaving behind only its reflection in the water. The king, believing his purpose had been fulfilled, returned to his capital. There, he assembled his forces and set out once more to wage war. However, as he advanced, he encountered various obstacles and calamities that he had never experienced before. His army suffered losses, and his own strength waned. Despondent and bewildered, the king returned to the sage for guidance. The sage said, "O King, you have committed a grave error. By sacrificing an image of the Divine, you have incurred his displeasure. Your defeat is certain because you have violated the sacred law. Realizing his mistake, the king repented deeply. He vowed to perform penance and to restore the statue to its rightful place. He sent messengers to search for the lost image, and after much wandering, they discovered it hidden in a remote cave. The king took the statue back to his capital and installed it in the temple with great ceremony. From that day forward, he ruled his kingdom with justice and compassion, abandoning all vices. Because of his devotion and rectitude, he eventually attained a state of peace and prosperity. Thus ends the story of the twenty-sixth statuette. It teaches that one should never disregard the divine or commit acts of sacrilege, for such actions lead to ruin. Instead, one should serve the Lord with sincerity and govern the world with righteousness.

The Story of the Twenty-sixth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king who possessed a great many horses. Among them was one horse that was exceedingly swift and powerful, yet it was difficult to tame. The king summoned his master trainers and said to them, "This horse is very fast and strong, but it will not submit to my will. You must find a way to break it. The trainers replied, "Your Majesty, we shall do our utmost to subdue this horse. Having spoken thus, they took the horse away and began their training. However, no matter how much they tried, they could not bring the horse under control. Finally, the trainers returned to the king and said, "Your Majesty, we have exhausted all our efforts, but we cannot tame this horse. We pray that you will permit us to depart. The king granted them leave. After some time had passed, the king went out for a hunt. He mounted that very horse and rode forth. As he galloped along, he saw a beautiful lake. Delighted by its beauty, he dismounted and entered the water to bathe. While he was bathing, the horse wandered off on its own and reached a dense forest. There, it encountered a lion. Terrified, the horse fled in panic and came to a clearing where it found a young man sitting beneath a tree. The horse approached the young man and stood before him. The young man, seeing the horse, spoke to it: "O horse, why have you come here? Tell me the reason for your arrival. The horse replied, "I am fleeing from a lion; please save me! The young man said, "Do not fear. I shall protect you. With these words, he took the horse and led it back to the king's palace. When the king returned from the hunt, he asked, "Where is my horse? His attendants replied, "Your Majesty, the horse has been brought back by a certain young man. The king summoned the young man and asked, "Why did you take my horse? The young man replied, "Your Majesty, while you were bathing in the lake, the horse wandered off and encountered a lion. Frightened, it fled and came to me. Out of compassion, I saved its life and brought it back to you. The king was deeply pleased and said, "I grant you whatever you desire. The young man requested, "Your Majesty, please grant me the hand of your daughter in marriage. The king consented and gave his daughter to him. Meanwhile, the horse remained with the young man. One day, the horse became ill and died. The young man performed the funeral rites for it and then set out again on a journey. As he traveled, he came across a large city. Inside the city, he saw a magnificent temple dedicated to the deity Maheśvara. He entered the temple and beheld the image of the god. At that moment, a voice from the sky spoke: "O youth, if you wish to obtain a kingdom, you must worship this image with devotion. The young man, hearing these words, worshipped the deity with great fervor. Because of his sincere devotion, the goddess appeared before him and said, "I am pleased with your devotion. Choose a boon. The young man replied, "O Goddess, I have no need for a kingdom. I ask only that you grant me the power to understand the speech of all animals. The goddess granted his request and vanished. Having received this boon, the young man lived happily with his wife. One day, as he was walking through the city, he heard the sound of a woman crying out in distress. He followed the sound and found a woman who had lost her child. She was weeping bitterly. The young man comforted her and said, "Do not grieve. I shall restore your child to life. He then recited a mantra, and the child rose up alive. The woman was overjoyed and thanked him profusely. As the young man continued his travels, he eventually arrived at a kingdom where the king was without an heir. The ministers sought a suitable person to become the new ruler. They heard of the young man’s virtues and his miraculous powers, so they sent messengers to invite him. The young man accepted the invitation and went to the kingdom. The people of the land welcomed him with great joy, and he was consecrated as king. Thus, through his wisdom, compassion, and devotion, the young man attained sovereignty and ruled the kingdom righteously. This is the story of the twenty-sixth statuette.

**Jainistic Recension of 26 JR:** The venerable Gautama addressed the Blessed One thus: “Blessed One, what is the fruit, what is the benefit of the practice of the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsā-vrata*)? The Blessed One replied: “O Gautama, the fruit, the benefit of the practice of the vow of non-violence is as follows: one does not kill living beings; one does not cause others to kill; one does not approve of the killing of others. One does not steal; one does not cause others to steal; one does not approve of the stealing of others. One does not commit sexual misconduct; one does not cause others to commit sexual misconduct; one does not approve of the sexual misconduct of others. One does not speak falsehood; one does not cause others to speak falsehood; one does not approve of the speaking of falsehood by others. One does not take that which is not given; one does not cause others to take what is not given; one does not approve of the taking of what is not given by others. One does not possess property; one does not cause others to possess property; one does not approve of the possession of property by others. One does not eat at improper times; one does not cause others to eat at improper times; one does not approve of the eating at improper times by others. One does not dance, sing, play musical instruments, or engage in other such diversions; one does not cause others to do so; one does not approve of such diversions by others. One does not wear garlands, apply perfumes, or adorn oneself with ornaments; one does not cause others to do so; one does not approve of such adornments by others. One does not sleep on high or large beds; one does not cause others to do so; one does not approve of sleeping on high or large beds by others. One does not accept gold and silver; one does not cause others to accept them; one does not approve of the acceptance of gold and silver by others. Furthermore, O Gautama, the practitioner of the vow of non-violence abandons all forms of injury to living beings, whether subtle or gross, whether mobile or immobile, whether born from eggs, wombs, sweat, or sprouts. The Story of the Twenty-sixth Statuette. Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāśakti who ruled over the city of Śrāvastī. He was powerful, possessed of great wealth, and governed his kingdom with righteousness. His queen was named Śaktimatī, and they had a son named Śaktideva, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. Now, it so happened that the king had a minister named Viṣṇudatta, who was wise, capable, and highly trusted. One day, while the king was seated in his assembly hall, the minister approached him and said: "Your Majesty, I have heard of a certain merchant's daughter named Ratnavatī, who is peerless in beauty and virtue. She would be a fitting consort for Prince Śaktideva. The king, being pleased with the proposal, sent messengers to summon the merchant. When the merchant arrived, the king granted him an audience and requested his daughter's hand for the prince. The merchant, out of respect for the king, agreed to the proposal. A grand marriage ceremony was then prepared. On the appointed day, the prince set out from the palace to meet his bride. As he traveled along the road, he encountered a group of wandering ascetics. Among them was a young woman named Kāmandakī, who was renowned for her wisdom and eloquence. Seeing the prince, she spoke to him with great charm and insight, captivating his heart with her words. Filled with wonder at her intellect and grace, the prince asked her to accompany him back to the city. Kāmandakī consented, and they returned together. Upon their arrival, the prince introduced her to his father, the king, and his mother, Queen Śaktimatī. They were both delighted by her presence and welcomed her as a guest. Meanwhile, the merchant's daughter, Ratnavatī, was anxiously awaiting the arrival of her husband. When she learned that the prince had brought a woman with him, she became jealous and suspicious. She began to plot against Kāmandakī, fearing that she might be a rival for her husband's affection. One night, while the prince was away on a hunting excursion, Ratnavatī conspired with her maidservant to cast Kāmandakī out of the palace. Under the pretext of a household dispute, they drove her away into the forest. Kāmandakī, however, was not one to be easily defeated; she fled into the wilderness and sought refuge with a group of forest-dwelling sages. Time passed, and the prince returned home. Finding Kāmandakī missing, he was filled with grief and remorse. He searched everywhere for her but found no trace. Meanwhile, Ratnavatī, believing herself secure, lived in luxury, unaware of the consequences of her actions. Months later, fate intervened. A caravan of merchants traveling through the forest stumbled upon Kāmandakī. Recognizing her wisdom and virtue, they took her along as their guide. The caravan eventually reached a distant land where a great festival was being held. There, Kāmandakī met a nobleman who was impressed by her character and offered her his protection. In due course, the prince, still mourning the loss of Kāmandakī, decided to travel abroad in search of her. He joined a merchant caravan and set out on his journey. By chance, the caravan crossed paths with the one led by the nobleman who had taken Kāmandakī under his care. The two groups met, and Kāmandakī was reunited with the prince. Overjoyed, the prince recounted his own sorrowful tale to her, and they pledged their eternal devotion to one another. Together, they returned to Śrāvastī, where they were received with great honor by the king and queen. Ratnavatī, seeing the reconciliation and the depth of the prince's love, felt a pang of conscience. She confessed her guilt and begged for forgiveness. From that day forward, the king’s household lived in harmony. The prince and Kāmandakī were married with great ceremony, and Ratnavatī, having learned her lesson, became a devoted wife. Thus, through wisdom and fortitude, Kāmandakī turned a potential tragedy into a story of enduring love and reconciliation. The moral of this tale is that true virtue and intelligence can overcome adversity, and that jealousy, when unchecked, leads to regret and ruin. **The Story of the Twenty-Seventh Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahābala who ruled over the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and possessed of immense wealth. However, he was utterly devoid of compassion and took pleasure in inflicting suffering upon others. One day, as the king was seated upon his throne, a merchant arrived before him. This merchant had been traveling from a distant land with a great caravan of goods. As he approached the royal court, he was seized by a sudden, violent fit of fever. Despite the best efforts of the physicians and the administration of various medicines, his condition did not improve; on the contrary, it grew worse by the moment. Seeing that the merchant’s life was ebbing away, the king ordered his servants to cast him out of the city, saying, "Let this wretch die outside my realm. As the merchant lay dying on the outskirts of the city, he began to reflect upon his past deeds. He thought to himself: "I have committed no great sin, yet I suffer this fate because of my greed for profit. Alas! What shall become of me? While he was thus lamenting, a certain holy man (sādhu) happened to pass by. Moved by pity, the ascetic sat beside the dying man and spoke these words of consolation: "Do not grieve, O merchant. Even in this state, you may still perform a meritorious act. The merchant, filled with hope, asked, "What must I do? The holy man replied, "If you have any remaining wealth, give it all in charity to the poor and the needy. Furthermore, offer prayers for the welfare of King Mahābala, for it is said that the merit of a gift given for the sake of another accrues to that person. The merchant, though weak, gathered what little strength he had left and distributed his remaining goods among the poor. Then, with a focused mind, he offered prayers for the king's long life and prosperity. At that very moment, the merchant passed away. Meanwhile, back in the palace, King Mahābala was suddenly stricken by a severe illness identical to that which had afflicted the merchant. His body burned with a high fever, and he suffered great pain. The physicians were at their wits' end, and the king’s condition grew critical. One night, while the king was lying in his bed, he saw a vision in a dream. A divine being appeared before him and said: "O King, you are suffering because of the evil karma you have incurred. You once cast a dying merchant out of your kingdom. Because of that act of cruelty, you now endure this agony. However, the merchant died while offering prayers for your well-being; therefore, if you repent and perform acts of merit, your suffering will cease. Startled by the vision, the king woke up and summoned his ministers. He told them everything that had occurred in his dream and commanded that messengers be sent to the outskirts of the city to inquire about the merchant’s death. When they returned and reported that the merchant had indeed died while praying for the king, the king was overcome with remorse. He realized the gravity of his own actions and resolved to atone for his sins. The king immediately issued a proclamation throughout the city, ordering that all prisoners be released and that alms be distributed to the poor. He then set out on a pilgrimage to sacred shrines and temples, performing acts of charity and penance. Through these virtuous deeds, the king’s illness gradually subsided, and he was restored to health. From that time forward, King Mahābala became known as a ruler of righteousness and compassion. He governed his kingdom with justice and ensured that no living being suffered under his rule. Thus ends the story of the twenty-seventh statuette. It teaches that even those in positions of power must beware of cruelty, for the consequences of one’s actions follow like a shadow. Only through repentance and the cultivation of virtue can one find peace and liberation from suffering.

28. The Story of the Twenty-Eighth Statuette: Vikrama Abolishes the Sacrifice of Men to a Bloody Goddess Southern Recension of 28 King Bhoja said: "O wise one, tell me another story. The statuette replied: "Listen, O King. In the city of Pāṭaliputra there lived a king named Vikramāditya. He was a man of great power, possessing all virtues, and a protector of his subjects. Once, while he was ruling the earth, a certain Brahmin came from a distant land and stood before the king. He said: 'O King, in the southern region there is a city called Kāñcī. There dwells a king named Śūdraka, who is a devotee of the god Śiva. He possesses a daughter named Madanasundarī, who is like a second Lakṣmī in beauty. She has been born as a result of a boon granted by the god Śiva. Now, in that city there is a temple of the goddess Caṇḍikā, who is blood-thirsty and fond of human sacrifice. Every year, on the day of the festival of the goddess, a man is sacrificed to her. The king himself goes there and offers a human being as an oblation. I have come here seeking my daughter; however, I am terrified of that goddess. Therefore, O King, please grant me your protection. Hearing this, King Vikrama summoned his minister and said: 'Go, O minister, and bring that maiden here at once. The minister went to the city of Kāñcī and brought the maiden to the presence of King Vikrama. When the maiden saw the king, she was struck with wonder at his beauty and fell in love with him. The king, too, beholding her, was filled with great joy. Then the king summoned the Brahmin and said: 'O Brahmin, take this maiden and go to your own country. I shall protect you from the danger of the goddess. Having received the maiden, the Brahmin departed for his home. But the king remained there, reflecting upon the power of the goddess. One night, while the king was awake, the goddess Caṇḍikā appeared before him in a terrible form and said: 'O King, why do you protect this maiden? Every year I require a human sacrifice. If you do not offer her to me, I shall destroy your kingdom and your life. Hearing these words, the king was undaunted. He bowed to the goddess and said: 'O Goddess, I do not desire to harm anyone. I am a protector of the helpless. If you truly desire a sacrifice, then let me offer myself to you instead of this maiden. The goddess was pleased by his selflessness and said: 'O King, I am satisfied with your courage. Ask for whatever boon you desire, and it shall be granted. The king replied: 'O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, then abolish forever the practice of human sacrifice in your temples throughout the world. The goddess agreed to his request and vanished. From that time forward, the custom of offering human sacrifices to the goddess Caṇḍikā was abolished by King Vikrama. The statuette concluded: "Thus, O King, did King Vikrama, through his compassion and wisdom, put an end to the cruel rite of human sacrifice."

**The Story of the Twenty-Ninth Statuette** Once upon a time, there was a king who possessed a great many horses. Among them was one horse that was exceptionally swift and powerful. This horse would travel vast distances in a single day, and because of its speed, it became the object of great affection for the king. One day, the king decided to test his horse’s speed against those of other kings. He sent messengers to various neighboring kingdoms, challenging their rulers to a race. The horse was adorned with golden trappings and a jeweled saddle, and it set out with great pride. As the race commenced, the horse galloped ahead of all the others, leaving them far behind. The king watched from the sidelines, filled with joy at his mount's prowess. However, as the day wore on, the horse began to show signs of exhaustion. It slowed its pace, and eventually, it fell behind. Seeing this, the king grew anxious. He urged his horse to pick up speed, but the animal was spent. The other kings, seeing their opportunity, overtook him and won the race. The king returned to his palace in shame, his pride wounded by the defeat of his beloved steed. That night, the king could not sleep. He sat upon his throne, brooding over his loss. Suddenly, he heard a voice from the darkness of the chamber: "O King, why do you grieve? Your horse was indeed swift, but it was burdened by the weight of your expectations. Had you allowed it to run freely, without the pressure of victory, it would have reached its full potential. Startled, the king turned to see no one there. Yet, the words lingered in his mind. He realized that his attachment to the horse’s performance had become a burden, stifling its natural vigor. From that day forward, the king ceased to demand constant triumph from his steed, allowing it to live according to its own nature. And so, the horse regained its former strength and joy, serving the king with renewed devotion. Thus ends the story of the twenty-ninth statuette. It teaches that when we place excessive weight upon our loved ones, we may inadvertently stifle their very essence. True care lies in providing freedom and support, rather than imposing the weight of our own desires.

The Story of the Twenty-Ninth Statuette: Vikrama’s Generosity Praised by a Bard Once, as King Vikrama was seated upon his throne, a bard approached him and said: “O King, listen to this ancient tale. In the city of Ujjayinī, there lived a king named Śrīdatta. He was renowned throughout the world for his boundless generosity. One day, a wandering bard arrived at his court and sang this verse: ‘In the land of Avanti, there dwells a king who is like a god; He bestows wealth upon those who ask, even if it be his own life. Upon hearing these words, the king summoned the bard and asked, ‘Is this true? The bard replied, ‘It is indeed true, O King. The king then reflected, ‘If I do not verify this, I shall be like one who has never seen the ocean. Therefore, I must test his claim. With this thought, he gave the bard a thousand gold coins and sent him away. The bard traveled through various lands until he reached the city of Ujjayinī. There, he entered the palace of King Śrīdatta and repeated the very same verse he had sung before King Vikrama. Hearing it, King Śrīdatta was deeply moved and exclaimed, ‘This is the voice of my own bard! He immediately summoned the bard and asked, ‘What did you say? The bard replied, ‘I sang the verse that praises your majesty’s fame. The king then rewarded him with ten thousand gold coins. As the bard was departing, the king called out to him, ‘Bard, wait! I have another task for you. The bard turned back and asked, ‘What is your command, O King? The king said, ‘Go to the city of Ayodhyā and find King Daśaratha. When you see him, sing this verse: ‘In the city of Ayodhyā, there dwells a king who is like a god; He bestows wealth upon those who ask, even if it be his own life. After many days of travel, he reached Ayodhyā and presented himself before King Daśaratha. He repeated the verse, and the king, recognizing his own work, bestowed upon him a great reward. When the bard returned to Ujjayinī, he related all that had occurred. King Śrīdatta was delighted and said, “Bard, you have performed a great service for me. Version MR The king, having heard those words of his son, was filled with great sorrow; he spoke these words to him, his voice choked with tears: "O son, do not grieve; this is the nature of all beings. All things that have come into existence must inevitably perish. Since you have been born into this world, you must surely face death. Therefore, O son, do not grieve; rather, perform your duty. Thus addressed by his father, the prince, though distressed, restrained his grief and spoke these words: "If it is certain that all beings must die, then why do you, O father, lament for me? If death is inevitable for all, then why do you not abandon your own body? If you yourself are subject to death, then what cause is there for you to grieve for me? Furthermore, if you think that I am dear to you because I am your son, then consider your own sons as well; they too are dear to you. If you love them, then why do you not protect them from death? If you say that their time has not yet come, then tell me when my time will arrive. If you say that I am young and therefore death does not yet touch me, then tell me how long this youth shall remain. Moreover, if you think that I am your son and therefore worthy of protection, then tell me who among the gods or men is not a son to someone else. If you say that I am your son because I was born from your body, then tell me whose son you yourself are. If you say that I am your son because I owe you a debt of gratitude, then tell me what service I can perform for you in return. Furthermore, if you think that I am your son because I am dependent on you, then tell me who is not dependent on someone else in this world. If you say that I am your son because I am born of your lineage, then tell me whose lineage you yourself belong to. If you say that I am your son because I am born of your wife, then tell me whose wife she is. Therefore, O king, since all beings are subject to birth and death, you should not grieve for me. Perform your royal duties, govern the earth, and protect your subjects according to dharma. Abandon this delusion and sorrow, and remain firm in your resolve. Having spoken thus, the prince fell silent. The king, hearing his son’s words, was overcome with even greater sorrow and wept aloud. He embraced his son and said: "O son, I know that all things are transient, yet my heart cannot endure this separation. Stay here for a short while longer, and then you may go wherever you wish. The prince replied: "If you truly know the truth of the world, then why do you speak such words? If you wish to see me, then look upon your own self; for you and I are both subject to the same fate. Do not let your mind be clouded by affection; rather, fix it upon the eternal. Thus exhorted by his son, the king, though deeply pained, composed himself and prepared to depart for the forest. Taking leave of his family and his kingdom, he set out on the path of renunciation, seeking the peace of liberation.

The Story of the Twenty-ninth Statuette. Once upon a time, there was a king who ruled over a vast kingdom. He possessed great wealth and power, yet he lacked a son. Desiring a son, the king performed various rites and made many offerings, but his wish remained unfulfilled. Then, the king heard that in a certain forest there lived a sage of great ascetic power. The king went to the sage and, having paid him due homage, said: "O Great Sage, I am childless and yearn for a son. Please grant me your blessing so that I may obtain one. The sage replied: "O King, it is not easy for you to obtain a son through mere ritual acts. However, if you can find a woman who possesses the thirty-two marks of excellence and give her to me as my wife, then I shall grant your wish. The king returned to his palace and summoned all the women of his court, saying: "Whosoever among you possesses the thirty-two marks of excellence, let her come before me. The Story of the Thirtieth Statuette Once upon a time, there was a king who possessed a great many horses. Among them was one horse that was exceedingly swift; its speed was such that it could not be matched by any other. The king was so fond of this horse that he never allowed it to go hungry or thirsty, nor did he ever let it suffer from exhaustion. One day, a certain man approached the king and said, "O King, your majesty possesses a horse that is the swiftest in all the world. I have a son who is a master of horsemanship; if you would allow him to ride this horse, I am certain he will bring it back to you in a single day. The king, being very fond of his horse, agreed to the man's proposal. He gave the horse to the man and his son. The father took the horse and rode it away for several days until they reached a place where there were no more villages or towns. There, the father said to his son, "Son, you must now take care of the horse yourself. I shall remain here and wait for you. The son replied, "Father, do not worry. I shall take good care of the horse and return to you safely. With these words, the father left his son with the horse and went off to find food and water for himself. Left alone, the young man began to think, "This horse is indeed very fast. If I ride it at full speed, I might reach home before my father does. But what if I ride it slowly? Then my father will surely catch up to me. Thinking thus, he decided to ride the horse at a moderate pace. As he traveled, he saw a beautiful grove of trees and thought, "I shall rest here for a while. So he dismounted, tied the horse to a tree, and sat down to rest. While he was resting, he fell asleep. Meanwhile, the father had found some food and water and was returning when he met another man on the road. That man asked him, "Where are you going? The father replied, "I am going to fetch my son and the horse. The man said, "Why do you not ride this horse? It is very fast. The father thought, "This man speaks the truth," and so he mounted the horse and rode off at full speed. When the young man woke up, he looked around but saw neither his father nor the horse. He searched everywhere but could find nothing. Finally, he mounted the horse and rode as fast as he could, thinking, "Perhaps my father has gone ahead of me. However, because he had already lost time resting, he was unable to catch up. As he rode along, he saw a large city and thought, "I shall enter this city and ask the people about my father. He entered the city and asked, "Have you seen a man with a horse like this? No one knew anything of him. He continued his search until he reached the palace of the king. There, he saw the king sitting on his throne. The young man approached the king and said, "O King, have you seen a man with a horse like this? The king replied, "I have not seen anyone like that. The young man then told the king everything that had happened. The king was amazed and said, "It is truly a wonder how you managed to come here without your father! The young man replied, "O King, it is because I was slow in riding the horse that I have come here. The king laughed and said, "You have been deceived by your own cleverness. Had you ridden the horse at full speed, you would have arrived long ago. The young man realized his mistake and felt ashamed. He returned to his father and apologized. His father said, "Son, you have learned a lesson today. One must always act with wisdom and not be led astray by mere appearances. Thus ends the story of the thirtieth statuette. It teaches that one should always exercise discernment and not be deceived by superficial impressions.

7. *kṣamāvān dharma-śīlaś ca* — One who is patient and of virtuous character; 8. *dayāvān sarva-jantuṣu* — Compassionate toward all living beings; 9. *maitrī-bhāva-samanvitaḥ* — Endowed with a disposition of loving-kindness; 10. *karuṇā-paricārakaḥ* — One who practices compassion; 11. *muditā-vihārī ca* — Dwelling in sympathetic joy; 12. *upekṣā-pariniṣṭhitaḥ* — Established in equanimity; 13. *jñāna-dhyāna-samāyuktaḥ* — Joined with knowledge and meditation; 14. *saṃvara-vrata-dhārakaḥ* — A bearer of the vows of restraint; 15. *tapasvī niḥspṛhaḥ sadā* — An ascetic always free from desire; 16. *bāhya-abhyantara-tapasi* — In external and internal austerity; The Story of the Thirty-First Statuette: Vikrama and the Vetāla (Southern Recension of 31) The King said: "O Vetāla, tell me, why did that king abandon his own wife and take another woman as his queen? The Vetāla replied: "O King, listen. In the city of Ujjayinī there was a king named Śūdraka. He was a man of great power, possessing a vast army, and he ruled the earth with justice. Once, while wandering through the forest for the sake of hunting, he saw a certain ascetic who had been practicing penance for twelve years. The king approached him and asked: 'O holy one, what is the purpose of this penance? What do you desire? The ascetic replied: 'O King, I am performing this penance desiring a son. May a son be born to me. The king said: 'O holy one, I shall grant you a son endowed with all virtues. However, you must first fulfill my request. The ascetic asked: 'What is your command, O King? The king said: 'I have a daughter-in-law who is exceedingly beautiful. Grant her to me. The ascetic replied: 'O King, I shall give her to you, but you must protect her well. Having agreed to this, the king took the daughter-in-law and went to his palace. There, he gave her to his chief queen, saying: 'This is the daughter-in-law of the ascetic; protect her well. Meanwhile, the ascetic returned to his hermitage and performed a sacrifice. From the sacrificial fire, a son was born to him, endowed with great splendor. When the boy grew up, the ascetic said to him: 'My son, go to the city of Ujjayinī and serve King Śūdraka. There you will obtain great wealth and enjoy every pleasure. The boy set out and reached the city of Ujjayinī. There he saw the king’s daughter-in-law, who was like a goddess. Seeing her, he was overcome by passion and thought: 'How can I obtain this woman? He then assumed the guise of a wandering mendicant and entered the king's palace. There he saw the daughter-in-law, who was seated upon a couch. Seeing her, he was struck by love and, approaching her, spoke these words: 'O lady, I am a wandering mendicant. I have come here seeking alms. Grant me food. The daughter-in-law, seeing him, felt compassion and gave him food. As she was giving it, she looked at him intently and fell deeply in love with him. She thought: 'Who is this handsome man? How can I obtain him? The mendicant, perceiving her affection, said: 'O lady, I am a wandering mendicant. I have no home. Where shall I stay? She replied: 'Stay here in this house. He stayed there, and they lived together in secret. One day, the king’s chief queen saw them together. Enraged, she went to the king and said: 'O King, this mendicant is violating your daughter-in-law. Hearing this, the king was filled with wrath. He ordered his servants: 'Seize that mendicant and bring him before me. The servants seized him and brought him to the king. The king, seeing him, said: 'O mendicant, why have you committed such a crime? Tell me the truth. The mendicant replied: 'O King, I am not a sinner. I am a servant of the ascetic. I have come here to serve you. I have done nothing wrong. The king, though hearing his words, did not believe him. Out of anger, he ordered his execution. As the executioners were leading him away to the place of execution, the mendicant cried out: 'O King, I am innocent! I have been deceived by this wicked woman! The king, hearing this, felt pity and said: 'Let him be released. The executioners released him. The mendicant then went to the ascetic and told him everything that had happened. The ascetic, hearing his account, was filled with grief and said: 'My son, you have been deceived by a wicked woman. You must go back and kill her. The mendicant returned to the city and found the daughter-in-law. He killed her and threw her into a well. Then he went to the ascetic and told him: 'Father, I have killed the woman and thrown her into a well. The ascetic, hearing this, was pleased and said: 'My son, you have done well. Now go and serve the king again.'

The Story of the Thirty-First Statuette. (sr) SR: The thirty-first statue said: "O King, listen to this story concerning a certain merchant's son who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, was subsequently reborn in the world of Brahmā. In the city of Śrāvastī, there lived a certain merchant’s son named Sudhana. He was handsome, virtuous, and endowed with great wealth. Having heard the Dharma from the Blessed One, he developed faith and took refuge in the Triple Gem. He maintained the five precepts and, with a devoted mind, offered food, clothing, and other requisites to the Saṅgha. One day, while traveling through the countryside, he encountered a forest fire. As the flames spread rapidly, he fled for his life. While running, he saw a monk sitting beneath a tree, absorbed in meditation. Filled with joy, Sudhana approached him and prostrated. The monk, seeing his pure intention, bestowed upon him the precepts of a lay follower and instructed him in the practice of mindfulness. Sudhana returned home and, with great diligence, practiced the teachings he had received. Through the power of his merit, he eventually attained the fruit of Arhatship. Having realized the exhaustion of all outflows, he lived in the bliss of liberation. After some time, he passed away and was reborn in the world of Brahmā. There, surrounded by the gods of that realm, he enjoyed celestial splendor. When the Blessed One, seated amidst the assembly of monks, recounted the various destinies of those who have passed away, he spoke of Sudhana’s attainment of Arhatship and his subsequent birth in the Brahma-world. The monks were filled with wonder and asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how did this merchant’s son, having attained such high spiritual realization, come to be born in the world of Brahmā? The Blessed One replied: "Monks, it is because Sudhana possessed a mind of pure faith and maintained the precepts without flaw. By the power of his merit and his devotion to the Triple Gem, he was able to transcend the human realm and attain rebirth among the gods of Brahmā. Thus, the Blessed One taught that even those who have attained the highest spiritual fruits can, through the force of their previous vows and meritorious deeds, be reborn in the higher realms. The monks, having heard this teaching, were greatly inspired and redoubled their efforts in the practice of the Dharma. The thirty-first statue concluded its tale. The King, having heard it, was filled with joy and praised the wisdom of the Buddha. He then commanded that the statue be placed in its proper position.
Thus ends the thirty-first story.

31. The Story of the Thirty-First Statuette Once upon a time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a king named Brahmadatta. He was powerful, wealthy, and possessed of great majesty. His kingdom was prosperous, his treasury full, and his realm free from strife. The king was devoted to dharma, truthful, and compassionate toward all beings. Now, this King Brahmadatta had a queen named Śrīmatī, who was beautiful, virtuous, and endowed with every auspicious quality. Together they ruled the kingdom with righteousness. One day, as the king sat upon his throne in the assembly hall, surrounded by his ministers and counselors, a messenger arrived from the frontier regions. Having prostrated himself before the king, he said: "Your Majesty, there is a certain merchant named Dhanapālita who has come from the city of Mathurā. He brings with him a most extraordinary object—a statue made of precious gems, the like of which has never been seen before. The king, being curious to see it, summoned the merchant at once. When the merchant arrived, he was ushered into the presence of the king. The king asked him, "Merchant, what is this marvelous thing you have brought? The merchant replied, "Great King, this is a statue of the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. It was carved by a master artisan from a single block of precious stone. It possesses such radiance that it illuminates the entire palace. The king, filled with wonder, ordered the statue to be brought into the inner apartments. There, amidst a multitude of lamps, the statue shone with a brilliance that surpassed even the light of the sun. The king gazed upon it for a long time, his heart filled with devotion. Then the king addressed his ministers: "This statue is truly wondrous. Who might have fashioned it? And how did it come into the possession of this merchant? A wise minister among them, well-versed in ancient lore, replied: "Your Majesty, in former times, during the reign of King Mahendrasena, there lived a master sculptor named Viśvakarman. He was skilled in the arts of metalwork, woodwork, and gemstone carving. Once, while wandering through the forest, he encountered a great mountain of precious stones. Taking one of the finest gems, he set out to create a likeness of the Buddha. After many years of labor, he finally completed the statue. However, as he was about to consecrate it, he fell ill and passed away. Before he died, he entrusted the statue to his son, saying, 'Son, this is a representation of the Teacher of the World. You must honor it with all your heart. The son followed his father's instructions, and eventually, the statue came into the hands of this merchant. The king, having heard this account, felt a deep sense of reverence for the Buddha. He decreed that the statue be enshrined in a magnificent temple and established a festival for its worship. From that day forth, the people of the city honored the statue with flowers, incense, and music, and the king himself paid homage to it daily. Thus ends the thirty-first story.

MR Bhaṭṭi becomes Vikrama’s Minister — Story 32 of MR Once upon a time, there was a king named Vikramāditya who ruled over the city of Ujjayinī. He was a man of great power and possessed of all virtues. One day, while wandering about in disguise, he came upon a certain Brahmin named Bhaṭṭi, who was extremely poor and suffering from hunger. Moved by compassion, the king gave him a large sum of gold coins and instructed him to live in comfort. Some time later, the king, still wandering in secret, saw that very same Bhaṭṭi walking along the road, carrying a heavy load of wood on his head. Seeing this, the king asked him, "O Brahmin, why do you carry such a burden of wood? Why have you fallen into such a state of poverty? The Brahmin replied with humility, "O King, it is because of my lack of merit and the exhaustion of my past deeds that I have become so destitute. Despite your former gift, I am once again reduced to this condition. The king, being of a noble heart, felt deep pity for him and thought, "This man must be made prosperous again. He then took Bhaṭṭi to his palace and appointed him as one of his ministers. From that time forward, Bhaṭṭi lived in great prosperity and became a trusted advisor to King Vikramāditya. Thus ends the thirty-second story of the *Mṛgāṅkacarita*.

Paragraph 1: The Conversion of King Vikrama to Jainism by Siddhasena Divākara In the city of Ujjayinī, there reigned a king named Śrī Vikramāditya, who was a devotee of the Jina and a protector of the Jain faith. One day, the renowned scholar Siddhasena Divākara arrived there. Hearing of his arrival, the king went out to meet him and, having paid his respects, invited him to his palace. The king said, "O Master, I have heard that you are a great poet and a master of logic. I wish to hear a verse from you. Siddhasena replied, "O King, I shall compose a verse for you, but it must be one that no one else has ever composed before. The king agreed, and Siddhasena immediately recited this verse: *Śaṅkhe śātakumbhastambhair bhāsvadbhāsvadgṛhe gṛhe | Karpūreṇa kṛtāmode modate ko na mānavaḥ?* "Who among men would not rejoice in a house where every chamber is filled with the fragrance of camphor, and where golden pillars shine like the sun? The king was delighted and offered him a reward. However, Siddhasena refused, saying, "I do not desire wealth; I seek only the opportunity to debate with you. The king consented, and they began to debate on various subjects. After many days, the king was defeated in argument. He said, "I am conquered; I accept your doctrine. Siddhasena replied, "A king should not be so easily defeated. You must undergo a test. He then presented the king with a bowl of water and said, "If you can drink this water without it touching your lips, then you are truly conquered. The king tried many times but could not do so. Finally, he asked for another test. Siddhasena gave him a mirror and said, "If you can see your reflection in this mirror without your eyes looking at it, then you are conquered. Again, the king failed. Then Siddhasena gave him a sword and said, "If you can cut this sword with this same sword, then you are conquered. Once more, the king failed. Finally, Siddhasena gave him a peacock feather and said, "If you can make this feather dance without touching it, then you are conquered. The king tried everything but could not succeed. Despairing, he said, "I am truly conquered. I surrender myself to your faith. Siddhasena then initiated the king into the Jain fold, and King Vikramāditya became a devoted follower of the Jina. Thus ended the conversion of King Vikrama through the power of Siddhasena Divākara.
While King Vikramāditya was thus ruling the kingdom, there arose another [account]:

Now, tell me, what further did that sage say? The Brahmin replied: "O King, listen attentively to what the sage said next. He spoke as follows: 'O King, there is a city named Śrāvastī, which is like the very abode of the gods. There dwells a king named Prasenajit, who is devoted to the welfare of his subjects. In that city lives a merchant named Dhanapati, who is exceedingly wealthy and possesses vast stores of grain and riches. He has a wife named Dhanaśrī, who is virtuous and endowed with all auspicious marks. To them was born a son named Dhanadatta, who was handsome, intelligent, and beloved by all. As he grew up, the youth became proficient in all the arts and sciences, and he was especially skilled in commerce. One day, while traveling abroad for trade, he reached a great forest. There, overcome by hunger and thirst, he lost his way. Wandering aimlessly, he came upon a hermitage where he beheld a sage seated beneath a tree. Bowing down in reverence, the youth approached him and asked: "O holy one, what is this forest? And how far is it from here to the city of Śrāvastī? The sage, perceiving the youth's distress, spoke these words of consolation: "O son, this is the Vindhya forest, a place of many dangers. However, do not fear; I shall guide you safely out of this wilderness. Having spoken thus, the sage led the youth through the thicket until they emerged on the edge of a vast lake. The sage then instructed him: "O youth, remain here for a few days and subsist on the fruits and roots of this forest. When you see a man emerge from the water, follow him and ask him the way to Śrāvastī. He will surely lead you there. With these instructions, the sage departed. The youth remained at the lakeside, living on wild fruits. After some time, a man emerged from the water, and the youth followed him. As they traveled together, the man eventually arrived at a city situated on the shore of the ocean. There, the youth saw a magnificent temple dedicated to Viṣṇu, adorned with gold and jewels. Entering the temple, he beheld a beautiful maiden sitting before an image of the Lord. She was radiant, possessed of exquisite beauty, and seemed like a goddess descended to earth. Approaching her with humility, the youth asked: "O lady, who are you? And why do you sit here alone? The maiden, looking upon him with a gentle smile, replied: "I am the daughter of the Nāga king Vāsuki, named Padmāvatī. My father has commanded me to marry a mortal who possesses great merit. Therefore, I have come here to test the hearts of those who visit this sacred place. You appear to be a man of noble character; pray, tell me your name and lineage. The youth, filled with joy, introduced himself and told her of his birth and adventures. Delighted by his story, she said: "If you truly wish to be my husband, then swear an oath of truth before this divine image. The youth agreed, and having taken the vow, he was united with her in marriage according to the rites prescribed for mortals and immortals. Story 31 (of manuscripts) of the Jainistic Recension: The Haunted House (JR) Once upon a time, there was a merchant’s son who lived in a certain city. He was handsome, wealthy, and possessed of great virtue. One day, while wandering about, he came across a dilapidated house standing in a desolate part of the town. It was filled with cobwebs, infested with rats, and its walls were crumbling. Yet, it stood there, seemingly inhabited by some unseen spirit. Filled with curiosity, the young man approached the house. As he drew near, he heard a faint sound of weeping and lamentation coming from within. Thinking it might be a place of refuge for those in distress, he resolved to enter. However, his friends and relatives tried to dissuade him, warning him that the house was cursed and haunted by malevolent spirits. Undaunted, the merchant’s son entered the house. Inside, he found a woman sitting in a corner, her face covered in tears. She was emaciated and dressed in tattered rags. When she saw him, she cried out, "O noble youth! I am a woman named Śrīmatī, the wife of a merchant. My husband has gone abroad on business, and I have been left alone here. A wicked neighbor, jealous of my beauty and wealth, cast a spell upon this house to drive me mad. I have been tormented by these evil spirits for many days, and I have no one to turn to for help. The merchant’s son comforted her, saying, "Do not fear, O lady. I shall protect you from these malevolent forces. With these words, he took her hand and led her out of the house. Once they were safe outside, he summoned his friends and arranged for her to stay with them until her husband returned. In due course, the merchant’s husband came home and was overjoyed to find his wife safe and sound. He thanked the merchant’s son profusely for saving her life and offered him his daughter in marriage as a token of gratitude. Thus, the merchant’s son married the beautiful maiden and lived happily ever after, having overcome the dangers of the haunted house through courage and compassion.
Thus ends the thirty-first story of the Jainistic recension.

Story 32 (of manuscripts) of the Jainistic Recension – The Poverty-Statue JR: Paragraph 1 In the city of Śrāvastī, there lived a merchant named Dhanasena. He was wealthy, possessing vast riches and abundant grain-stores. Yet, despite his fortune, he was extremely miserly; he never gave anything away, not even a single coin, and he was constantly anxious about the depletion of his wealth. One day, while wandering through the marketplace, he saw a statue of a man carved from wood, representing poverty. It was depicted with a haggard face, tattered rags, and a body so emaciated that its veins were clearly visible. Seeing this, the merchant thought to himself, "This figure truly represents my own condition! Though I possess great wealth, I am no different from a pauper because of my stinginess. Filled with remorse, he resolved to abandon his miserliness. He went to a temple and made a vow: "If I am to be freed from this poverty, may I become as wealthy as the god Kubera, the Lord of Treasures. Having made this solemn declaration, he began to practice generosity on a grand scale. He distributed alms to the poor, supported the monks, and gave gifts to all who came seeking help. As a result of his virtuous deeds, his wealth increased manifold. His granaries overflowed, and his treasuries were filled to the brim. The people of the city marveled at his sudden prosperity and spoke of him as one who had been transformed by his own charity. Thus, the merchant Dhanasena became famous throughout the land as a man who had conquered poverty through the power of giving.
